title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

            - '\chrome.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling

description: |

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Armored Likho digging a snake pit: inside the covert BusySnake Stealer campaign

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-03 17 use cases 11 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An inside look at the active Armored Likho APT campaign. The attackers are using spear-phishing, AI-generated loaders, and a new Python-based tool, BusySnake Stealer, to target organizations in Russia, Kazakhstan, and Brazil.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ZDI-CAN-25373 (CVE-2025-9491) LNK spawning PowerShell to fetch BusySnake loader · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Armored Likho digging a snake pit: inside the covert BusySnake Stealer campaign
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BusySnake NSIS dropper: pnx.exe injected from Temp\ns*.tmp staging folder · [LLM] BusySnake Python stealer executed from %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper (module.pyw) · [LLM] BusySnake VBScript persistence: wh_selfdelete.vbs / run.vbs in WindowsHelper · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BusySnake reverse SSH tunnel: ssh.exe -R launched by bundled Python payload · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
BusySnake NSIS dropper: pnx.exe injected from Temp\ns*.tmp staging folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the Armored Likho NSIS self-extracting dropper (e.g. psihologicheskiy_test.exe) writing and launching the legitimate binary pnx.exe from its temporary ns*.tmp extraction directory, into which the malicious loader is code-injected. This is article-specific because pnx.exe running out of an NSIS Temp folder is the first on-host execution artifact of this chain. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article string $temp\nsn5531.tmp\pnx.exe generalised to the NSIS ns*.tmp pattern; pnx.exe executing from an NSIS temp folder is a narrow, high-fidelity artifact of this dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/armored-likho-targets-government.html • https://www.securityweek.com/armored-likho-apt-targeting-government-electric-power-entities/
ATT&CKT1055 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Panasonic/other software shipping a 'pnx.exe' from a permanent install path (excluded here by the Temp\ns*.tmp path anchor)
  • Security researcher/malware analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • NSIS-based legitimate installers that coincidentally extract a binary named pnx.exe to Temp
  • EDR test/red-team emulation of this exact chain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the pnx.exe hash against the sample and identify the parent NSIS SFX (e.g. psihologicheskiy_test.exe) and the originating archive/email. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the pnx.exe process tree, and preserve the ns*.tmp folder for forensics before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper creation, module.pyw, run.vbs/wh_selfdelete.vbs, and outbound GitHub payload pulls; sweep the fleet for the same pnx.exe path.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pnx.exe"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\Temp\\ns[a-z0-9]+\.tmp\\pnx\.exe$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\Temp\\ns[a-z0-9]+\.tmp\\pnx\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BusySnake Python stealer executed from %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper (module.pyw) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the BusySnake Stealer primary payload — module.pyw run by a bundled Python 3.12 interpreter from the malware's %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper working directory. This is article-specific: the actor stages its own python.exe/pythonw.exe, get-pip.py and module.pyw under WindowsHelper and runs the .pyw headless. Rationale: Anchors on the exact staging path $appdata\WindowsHelper and the payload filename module.pyw; a self-contained Python interpreter running a .pyw from an AppData WindowsHelper folder is not seen in benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/armored-likho-targets-government.html • https://gbhackers.com/busysnake-stealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally installed to a folder literally named WindowsHelper (rare)
  • Developer running an embedded/portable Python distribution from an AppData path for a personal script
  • Malware analyst re-running the extracted payload in a lab
  • Software using PyInstaller/embedded Python that names a script module.pyw (very rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","pycharm64.exe","devenv.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture module.pyw and the WindowsHelper directory contents, confirm PyArmor packing and the bundled python.zip/get-pip.py provenance. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the pythonw.exe tree, and disable/delete the associated 5-minute scheduled task. 3) Hunt: pull browser-credential and cookie access on the host (Firefox/Chromium profile reads), outbound C2, and any ssh.exe reverse-tunnel; sweep fleet for %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\WindowsHelper\" or (ProcessCommandLine has "module.pyw" and ProcessCommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\python.exe","\\pythonw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has @"\WindowsHelper\" or (CommandLine has "module.pyw" and CommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BusySnake VBScript persistence: wh_selfdelete.vbs / run.vbs in WindowsHelper AIInstallation High
Hunts the BusySnake persistence and cleanup VBScripts — wh_selfdelete.vbs (wipes the pnx.exe loader) and run.vbs (launches module.pyw and registers the 5-minute scheduled task) — executed by wscript/cscript from the %APPDATA%\WindowsHelper directory. Article-specific by the unique script names and staging path. Rationale: wh_selfdelete.vbs is a unique, actor-specific filename; run.vbs is scoped with the WindowsHelper staging path to keep it high-fidelity. Directly maps to the article's named persistence/cleanup scripts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/armored-likho-targets-government.html
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal legacy VBScript coincidentally named run.vbs (mitigated by the WindowsHelper path requirement)
  • Login-script or SCCM automation invoking wscript with a same-named script from a different path
  • Malware analyst re-detonating the extracted scripts
  • Backup/uninstaller tooling that self-deletes via a VBS (would not match the unique wh_selfdelete.vbs name)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\CCM"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the VBS contents and the scheduled-task definition it created (look for the 5-minute recurrence launching module.pyw). 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task and the WindowsHelper directory, isolate the host, and block re-creation. 3) Hunt: verify whether wh_selfdelete.vbs already wiped the pnx.exe loader (check DeviceFileEvents FileDeleted), and pivot to credential/cookie theft and outbound C2 on the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "wh_selfdelete.vbs" or (ProcessCommandLine has "run.vbs" and ProcessCommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has "wh_selfdelete.vbs" or (CommandLine has "run.vbs" and CommandLine has "WindowsHelper")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ZDI-CAN-25373 (CVE-2025-9491) LNK spawning PowerShell to fetch BusySnake loader AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Armored Likho LNK infection vector: a malicious shortcut abusing CVE-2025-9491/ZDI-CAN-25373 (whitespace-padded hidden arguments) launched via Explorer, spawning PowerShell that downloads the loader and its python.zip/data.zip/get-pip.py package into WindowsHelper. Article-specific by the parent (explorer→powershell from LNK) plus the named payload artifacts. Rationale: Combines the CVE-2025-9491 LNK vector (Explorer-parented PowerShell) with the article's named loader-package artifacts (python.zip, data.zip, get-pip.py, WindowsHelper), which are specific to this chain rather than generic download cradles. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9491 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/10/31/zdi-can-25373-cve-2025-9491-exploited-again/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/IT shortcut that legitimately invokes PowerShell to fetch a zip package (rare and unlikely to reference these exact names)
  • Software updater launched from a Start-Menu LNK downloading a data.zip
  • Red-team/purple-team emulation of the LNK chain
  • User double-clicking a benign .lnk that runs a packaging script referencing get-pip.py
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr","DownloadFile","DownloadString","curl","wget","Start-BitsTransfer","http")
Response runbook
1) Triage: recover the LNK file and inspect its full Target/arguments for whitespace-padded hidden commands (CVE-2025-9491); identify the download URL(s) and originating email/archive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the PowerShell tree, block the download domains at proxy/DNS, and quarantine the LNK and delivered archive. 3) Hunt: search mail/gateway for the sibling lure archives (zayavka_*.rar, *_psihologicheskiy_test.zip), and pivot to WindowsHelper staging and scheduled-task persistence fleet-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("python.zip","data.zip","get-pip.py","WindowsHelper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("python.zip","data.zip","get-pip.py","WindowsHelper")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BusySnake reverse SSH tunnel: ssh.exe -R launched by bundled Python payload AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the BusySnake reverse-SSH-tunneling remote-access capability (successor to the group's Go2Tunnel usage): an ssh.exe reverse-tunnel (-R) process spawned by the malware's Python interpreter or from the WindowsHelper working directory. Article-specific by the parent-process pivot on the BusySnake payload rather than a generic ssh usage. Rationale: Uses the article's reverse-SSH-tunnel capability and pivots on the BusySnake Python payload (pythonw.exe / module.pyw / WindowsHelper) as parent, so it fires on attacker-driven tunnels rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/busysnake-stealer-malware/ • https://www.securityweek.com/armored-likho-apt-targeting-government-electric-power-entities/
ATT&CKT1572 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/DevOps engineer running Python automation (Fabric, Ansible, paramiko wrappers) that shells out to ssh -R for legitimate tunneling
  • CI/CD agent using a Python build script to open a reverse tunnel to a jump host
  • Data scientist using a Python-launched ssh -R for remote port forwarding to a lab box
  • Legitimate portable Python tool that manages SSH tunnels
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","fabric","paramiko")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the ssh.exe command line to identify the remote tunnel endpoint (host/port) and confirm the parent is the BusySnake pythonw.exe/module.pyw. 2) Contain: kill the ssh.exe and parent Python process, isolate the host, and block the tunnel destination IP/port at the firewall. 3) Hunt: enumerate all reverse-tunnel destinations across the fleet, correlate with WindowsHelper staging and credential/cookie theft, and review for lateral movement through the tunnel.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-R(\s|$)"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "module.pyw" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\WindowsHelper\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-R(\s|$)"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\python.exe","\\pythonw.exe") or CommandLine has "WindowsHelper"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

PamStealer Uses Fake Maccy Sites and PAM Checks to Steal Mac Login Passwords

The Hacker News
2026-07-03 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new macOS information stealer called PamStealer that employs a series of clever tricks to infect systems and siphon sensitive data. The stealer, discovered by Jamf Threat Labs, is distributed as a compiled AppleScript (.scpt) file impersonating Maccy, a legitimate open-source clipboard manager. It has been codenamed PamStealer owing to its ability to

Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Connection to PamStealer fake Maccy typosquat domains (maccyapp[.]com / .net) AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution or HTTP connections to the lookalike Maccy distribution sites that host the PamStealer .dmg/.scpt dropper. These domains are hardcoded delivery IOCs confirmed by Jamf and the Maccy developer, so any resolution from a corporate Mac is a delivery-stage hit. Rationale: Uses the exact typosquat delivery domains (maccyapp[.]com, maccyapp[.]net) confirmed by both Jamf Threat Labs and the legitimate Maccy developer's warning; the official site is maccy.app so any hit on maccyapp.* is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/pamstealer-uses-fake-maccy-sites-and.html
ATT&CKT1189 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst intentionally browsing the malicious domain for analysis
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment engine pre-resolving IOC domains from a sandbox VM
  • URL-detonation appliance following the link on the org's behalf
  • A user who bookmarked the fake site before takedown re-visiting it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("com.apple.XPCDeviceDiscovery","mdworker_shared") and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox-mac","malware-analysis-vm")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the host and user that resolved maccyapp.com/.net; check whether a .dmg or Maccy.scpt was subsequently written to Downloads and whether osascript/Script Editor launched. 2. Contain: isolate the endpoint if a payload download followed the resolution; block maccyapp.com/.net and avenger-sync.live at the proxy/DNS. 3. Hunt: pivot the same host for osascript reaching the internet, a Finder/System Settings binary running outside /System, and new LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plists.

osascript / Script Editor making outbound internet connection (PamStealer JXA downloader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the PamStealer execution stage where a compiled AppleScript run in Script Editor executes a self-contained JXA downloader that stages the Rust Mach-O payload using native Objective-C networking APIs. osascript/Script Editor reaching the public internet is abnormal and maps directly to the article's payload-staging behaviour (no curl/zsh is used). Rationale: Article states the JXA downloader fetches/stages the payload via native Objective-C APIs launched from Script Editor (Cmd+R) rather than curl/zsh; osascript/Script Editor egressing to a public IP is the cleanest process-anchored pivot for that stage. Sentinel left blank because macOS osascript-initiated network events are not carried by the Windows/ASIM network tables in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/02/new-mac-infostealer-confirms-stolen-passwords-before-stealing-data
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.002 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin AppleScript/JXA automation that calls a web API or Slack/Jira webhook
  • MDM or Jamf self-service scripts using osascript to fetch config
  • Developer testing a JXA script that downloads a resource
  • Backup/sync utilities that shell through osascript to an update endpoint
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "slack.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith "jamfcloud.com" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "/Library/Application Support/JAMF"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the remote host; determine if the destination is a known-good API or an unfamiliar IP/domain, and whether a Mach-O was written to Downloads/tmp immediately after. 2. Contain: isolate the host and kill the osascript/Script Editor process tree if the destination is unknown or resolves to avenger-sync.live infrastructure. 3. Hunt: look on the same host for a Finder-named binary executing from a non-/System path and new login-item plists created shortly after the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("osascript","Script Editor")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

PamStealer encrypted exfiltration to avenger-sync[.]live AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound connections to the PamStealer command-and-control / exfiltration endpoint avenger-sync[.]live, to which the Rust second stage sends encrypted browser data, wallet data, iCloud Keychain secrets and the captured login password over HTTP. This is a hardcoded C2 IOC corroborated across sources. Rationale: avenger-sync[.]live is the confirmed exfiltration endpoint (Jamf notes it aligns with the avngr/avenger delivery infrastructure across the sample set); a resolution or connection is a strong post-collection actions-on-objective signal. Finder or System Settings Mach-O executing from non-system path (PamStealer masquerade) AIInstallation High
Hunts the PamStealer second stage, a Rust arm64 Mach-O that masquerades as Finder.app, and the bundled helper that impersonates System Settings for persistence. Legitimate Finder and System Settings only execute from under /System/, so a process with those names running from a user-writable path is a direct masquerade hit. Rationale: Article and Jamf confirm the Rust second stage masquerades as Finder.app and a bundled arm64 Mach-O impersonates System Settings; the legitimate binaries live only under /System/Library/CoreServices and /System/Applications, so name-match plus non-/System path is high-fidelity with negligible legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/pamstealer-uses-fake-maccy-sites-and.html
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer building a project whose output binary happens to be named 'Finder' running from a build/DerivedData path
  • QA harness copying System Settings.app to a staging path for automation
  • Backup restore staging an app bundle to /Users/Shared before moving it
  • A renamed diagnostic tool coincidentally named 'Finder' in a user home directory
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "/Applications/" and FolderPath !has "/DerivedData/" and FolderPath !has "/Xcode/"
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the FolderPath, SHA256 and parent process; verify the binary is not code-signed by Apple and check the path (Downloads, /tmp, /var/folders, ~/Library indicate malware). 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the Mach-O; block avenger-sync.live and the maccyapp.* domains. 3. Hunt: on the same host look for the osascript JXA download that preceded it, new LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plists, and SMAppService login-item registration; sweep the fleet for the same SHA256.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Finder","System Settings")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/System/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/Finder" or TargetProcessName endswith "/System Settings"
| where not(TargetProcessName startswith "/System/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Login-item persistence plist written by non-Apple process (PamStealer SMAppService/legacy) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PamStealer's persistence: the Rust stage registers its Finder-masquerading bundle as a login item both via the modern SMAppService API and via a helper written to /tmp that adds a legacy login item. This surfaces LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist creation authored by a process running outside Apple/system paths. Rationale: Jamf confirms PamStealer persists by registering its Finder bundle as a login item via SMAppService and via a /tmp helper that writes a legacy login item; scoping plist creation in LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons to non-Apple authoring processes captures that without alerting on Apple/installer-managed persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pamstealer-macos-infostealer-applescript-rust/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/02/new-mac-infostealer-confirms-stolen-passwords-before-stealing-data
ATT&CKT1547.015 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party app (Dropbox, Zoom, Docker) installing its own LaunchAgent on first run
  • Homebrew services writing a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist
  • Jamf/MDM deploying a managed LaunchDaemon
  • A developer's build script installing a helper daemon during testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Dropbox","zoom.us","Docker","brew","jamf") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Applications/"
Response runbook
1. Triage: read the created plist's ProgramArguments and the authoring process path; a plist pointing at a Finder/System Settings binary in Downloads, /tmp or ~/Library is malicious. 2. Contain: isolate the host, unload and delete the offending plist, remove the login item, and quarantine the referenced Mach-O. 3. Hunt: correlate with the preceding osascript network egress and Finder-masquerade execution on the same host, and sweep the fleet for identical plist ProgramArguments or the same referenced binary hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/System/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Library/Apple/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".plist"
| where not(ActingProcessName startswith "/System/") and not(ActingProcessName startswith "/usr/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.action=created AND Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path IN ("*/Library/LaunchAgents/*","*/Library/LaunchDaemons/*") AND Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="*.plist" by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest, Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name, Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path, Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-02 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A look inside the reverse-engineering journey of building the first RDP client outside of Windows to support WebAuthn redirection. The post How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Likely
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — How We Added WebAuthn to a Browser-Based RDP Client
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.
let ioc = "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67";
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ioc or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ioc
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", Account=AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where FolderPath has ioc or FileName has ioc or FolderPath has "tj-actions/changed-files"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", Account=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=FolderPath, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
