Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Org-wide DNS lookups to TeamPCP campaign domains (Trivy / Checkmarx KICS / LiteLLM) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Process memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem targeting GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (TeamPCP Trivy stealer) · [LLM] Exfiltration to TeamPCP typosquat C2 scan.aquasecurtiy.org / stealer IPs from CI runner · [LLM] GitHub-native fallback exfil: creation of public 'tpcp-docs' repo by TeamPCP stealer
Process memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem targeting GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (TeamPCP Trivy stealer) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the TeamPCP credential-stealer's core collection step: a payload process reading /proc/<numeric-pid>/mem to scrape marked secrets ({"value":...,"isSecret":true}) out of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process memory. The numeric-PID regex excludes benign /proc/self/mem access, making cross-process memory reads on a CI runner a high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's literal code block `/proc/pid/mem` and the Runner.Worker target; the numeric-PID regex is the discriminator (legit /proc/self/mem is excluded). Aqua's GHSA advisory and Microsoft's guidance both confirm the stealer reads /proc/<pid>/mem from Runner.Worker searching for {"value":...,"isSecret":true}. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/SRE running gdb or gcore to capture a core dump during CI debugging
  • Memory-forensics tooling (AVML, LiME, volatility helpers) invoked in an incident-response pipeline
  • Performance profilers (perf, valgrind, heaptrack) attaching to a target PID
  • Language-runtime crash handlers that snapshot another process's memory
  • Container runtime health/introspection tools reading /proc/<pid>/mem of a monitored child
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","valgrind","criu","gcore","perf","heaptrack")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm the reader is a runner-spawned interpreter (python/node/sh) and the target PID resolves to Runner.Worker, not a debugger the dev launched. Check the runner's checked-out action refs for aquasecurity/trivy-action or setup-trivy. 2) Contain: cancel/isolate the CI job, revoke the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN and any cloud creds (AWS/GCP/Azure), and rotate every secret the workflow could read — assume exposure. 3) Hunt: pivot to that host's egress for scan.aquasecurtiy.org / 45.148.10.212 and to any process referencing 'tpcp-docs'; sweep all repos for the compromised action tags.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","valgrind","criu","gcore","perf")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where TargetProcessName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","valgrind","criu","gcore","perf")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exfiltration to TeamPCP typosquat C2 scan.aquasecurtiy.org / stealer IPs from CI runner AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the TeamPCP stealer's primary exfil: an HTTPS POST of AES/RSA-wrapped secrets to the typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org (mimics aquasecurity.com) resolving to 45.148.10.212, plus the campaign's additional stealer IPs. Any connection to this fixed attacker infrastructure is a confirmed compromise. Rationale: Uses the exact typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org and IP 45.148.10.212 named in the article body, plus the two campaign IPs from the IOC bundle. Aqua GHSA, Wiz and CrowdStrike all confirm scan.aquasecurtiy.org → 45.148.10.212 as the primary HTTPS-POST exfil channel. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/teampcp-supply-chain-attack-campaign-targets-trivy-checkmarx-kics-and-litellm-potential-downstream-impact-to-additional-projects/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An analyst or sandbox intentionally detonating the sample and beaconing to the C2 during research
  • A DNS-sinkhole or threat-intel scanner that resolves/probes the typosquat domain for tracking
  • IOC-validation tooling that curls the domain to confirm takedown status
  • Threat-hunt reproduction traffic generated during tabletop exercises
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/runner and the InitiatingProcess that opened the socket; confirm it is a CI job using a compromised trivy-action/setup-trivy or KICS tag. Because payloads are AES-256+RSA-4096 wrapped, do not rely on packet inspection — the destination alone is the verdict. 2) Contain: block the domain and all three IPs at the egress proxy/firewall, kill the job, and immediately rotate every secret reachable by that workflow (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud keys, registry creds). 3) Hunt: search all runners for /proc/<pid>/mem reads (UC1) and for the 'tpcp-docs' fallback (UC4), and enumerate every repo referencing the poisoned actions.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "scan.aquasecurtiy.org"
     or RemoteIP in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
     or DestinationHostName =~ "scan.aquasecurtiy.org"
     or RequestURL has "scan.aquasecurtiy.org"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP,
          DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Org-wide DNS lookups to TeamPCP campaign domains (Trivy / Checkmarx KICS / LiteLLM) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution of the full TeamPCP campaign domain set spanning the Trivy exfil host, the Checkmarx KICS lures (checkmarx.zone, audit.checkmarx.cx), the LiteLLM PyPI stealer C2 (models.litellm.cloud), and the Internet Computer canister fallback. Distinct from the runner-egress detection: this is an org-wide DNS pivot that catches any host touched by any arm of the campaign. Rationale: Combines the article's exfil domain with the pre-extracted campaign IOC domains (checkmarx.zone, audit.checkmarx.cx, models.litellm.cloud, and the full ICP canister host). Arctic Wolf and Kaspersky both attribute the Checkmarx-KICS and LiteLLM PyPI stealers to the same TeamPCP actor, so a hit on any of these is campaign-linked. Datadog left empty — the provided linux sources expose no DNS-question field. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/teampcp-supply-chain-attack-campaign-targets-trivy-checkmarx-kics-and-litellm-potential-downstream-impact-to-additional-projects/ • https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/critical-supply-chain-attack-trivy-litellm-checkmarx-teampcp/55510/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment platforms resolving the IOC domains for tracking/takedown monitoring
  • Security researchers detonating campaign samples in a lab that shares DNS telemetry
  • A legitimate developer typo'ing aquasecurity.com and hitting the typosquat once (single, non-repeating query)
  • Passive-DNS or brand-protection scanners crawling the typosquat namespace
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which host/user resolved the domain and the initiating process; determine which campaign arm it maps to (Trivy runner, Checkmarx KICS, or a LiteLLM/PyPI install). 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domain org-wide, isolate the resolving host, and rotate credentials that host or its pipelines could reach. 3) Hunt: for CI hosts pivot to UC1 (/proc/mem) and UC4 (tpcp-docs); for developer endpoints, inspect recent pip installs of litellm/telnyx and Python process ancestry for the stealer.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub-native fallback exfil: creation of public 'tpcp-docs' repo by TeamPCP stealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the stealer's fallback exfil channel documented by second sources: when scan.aquasecurtiy.org is unreachable and INPUT_GITHUB_PAT is present, the payload creates a public repo named tpcp-docs and uploads stolen data as release assets. Any process on a runner referencing 'tpcp-docs' (via git/gh/curl to api.github.com) is a unique, high-fidelity attacker artifact. Rationale: The unique attacker artifact 'tpcp-docs' (public repo name for the GitHub-native fallback exfil) has near-zero benign collision. Not in the article body but confirmed by Aqua's GHSA advisory, Microsoft's detection guidance ("look for public repositories named tpcp-docs"), and NVD remediation notes — so it is corroborated by multiple second sources and shipped accordingly. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A responder or researcher naming a scratch/IOC repo 'tpcp-docs' while investigating this campaign
  • A takedown/monitoring script that references the attacker repo name to check for its existence
  • Internal detection-engineering test harnesses that seed the string 'tpcp-docs' to validate this rule
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent process; confirm it is a git/gh/curl invocation creating or pushing to a public repo named tpcp-docs from a CI runner. Query the org's GitHub for any repo named tpcp-docs and delete/quarantine. 2) Contain: revoke the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN and any PAT (INPUT_GITHUB_PAT) exposed to the job, delete the attacker repo and its release assets, and rotate all reachable secrets. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (/proc/mem read) and UC2/UC3 (C2 egress) on the same host, and audit all workflows using aquasecurity/trivy-action, aquasecurity/setup-trivy, and Checkmarx KICS during the Mar 19–22 window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "tpcp-docs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "tpcp-docs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

Google Disrupts NetNut Residential Proxy Network Spanning 2 Million Home Devices

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 7 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Google has significantly degraded NetNut, one of the biggest networks that turns home devices into rented relays for other people's traffic. Working with the FBI, Lumen, and others, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)&nbsp;said this week&nbsp;it had reduced the network's pool of usable devices by millions. Google identifies NetNut, also tracked as Popa, as a network spread across home

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1528
Domainsnetnut.com netnut.io

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Enterprise asset contacting NetNut/Popa residential-proxy gateway (netnut.com/netnut.io) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Enterprise asset contacting NetNut/Popa residential-proxy gateway (netnut.com/netnut.io) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts managed endpoints resolving or connecting to the NetNut (aka Popa) commercial proxy gateway domains named in the article. On a corporate asset this indicates either an embedded NetNut SDK/proxyware component phoning home (turning the host into a rented exit node) or an insider routing traffic through the seized residential-proxy service — neither of which is legitimate enterprise traffic. Rationale: Uses the two concrete IOC domains (netnut.com, netnut.io) named in the article as the only high-fidelity anchor; corroborated by Google Cloud GTIG blog and KrebsOnSecurity confirming NetNut=Popa and the SDK-based exit-node model, though neither disclosed C2 domains/package names, so the gateway domains are the sole reliable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/google-continued-disruption-residential-proxy-networks/ • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/ • https://cybernews.com/news/google-fbi-disrupt-netnut-botnet-2-million-devices/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst browsing netnut.com to read the FBI seizure notice
  • Marketing/ad-verification or QA team legitimately evaluating a residential-proxy service for geo-testing
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox or web crawler visiting the domain from a lab subnet
  • SOC analyst pivoting on the IOC and clicking the domain during triage
  • Corporate DNS resolver forwarding a downstream user's one-off lookup
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process/host — is the connection browser-driven (likely a human visiting the site) or from a non-browser/service process (strong proxyware/SDK signal)? Check whether the host is a managed asset vs a lab/sandbox and whether contacts are repeated/beaconing vs a single lookup. 2) Contain: If a non-browser process is beaconing, isolate the host, block netnut.com/netnut.io and resolved IPs at the proxy/firewall, and quarantine the associated binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: Sweep the environment for the same process hash and for other known bandwidth-sharing/proxyware domains; review the host for unauthorized 'earn-money-for-bandwidth' apps and check whether it acted as an exit node (unexpected inbound/relayed connections) or was co-opted into Mirai/Badbox-style activity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,10), SampleProc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Connections desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), Responses=make_set(DnsResponseName,10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by Queries desc
title: NetNut/Popa Residential Proxy Gateway DNS Lookup
id: 6f3b1c8a-2e4d-4a7f-9c1b-8a0d5e2f7b91
description: Detects DNS resolution of the NetNut (Popa) residential-proxy gateway domains from an enterprise host, indicating proxyware/SDK phone-home or insider use of the seized proxy service.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/google-disrupts-netnut-residential.html
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/google-continued-disruption-residential-proxy-networks/
  - https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/03

  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:

    QueryName|endswith:
      - 'netnut.com'
      - 'netnut.io'
  condition: selection

  - Security researcher or threat-intel analyst browsing the vendor site
  - Legitimate geo-testing / ad-verification teams evaluating the proxy service

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*netnut.com OR *netnut.io OR *NetNut.com OR *NetNut.io)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| sort(count, order=desc)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.record_type) as record_type from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*netnut.com" OR DNS.query="*netnut.io") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest host | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.record_type) as record_type from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*netnut.com" OR DNS.query="*netnut.io") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest host | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15:9443 · [LLM] Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) deployment for persistent covert access · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anubis exfiltration tooling: rclone/s5cmd/S3 Browser/WinSCP cloud transfer · [LLM] Anubis encryptor /WIPEMODE destructive command execution · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15:9443 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the hardcoded command-and-control channel of The Gentlemen RaaS Go/Yamux backdoor, which opens a persistent bidirectional TCP session to 81.177.215.15 on port 9443 and executes operator commands via cmd.exe or opens a SOCKS proxy. The fixed IP+port pair makes this a high-fidelity network IOC. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 tuple 81.177.215.15:9443 confirmed by Kaspersky Securelist as The Gentlemen's Yamux Go backdoor endpoint — a fixed IP+port is one of the highest-fidelity network IOCs available. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1095 T1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation host deliberately connecting to the IOC
  • Security researcher or IR team validating the indicator
  • Shared NAT egress where a single benign host and a compromised host both egress the same public IP (only affects source attribution, not the destination match)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process on the connecting host (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) — a Go binary in %TEMP%/%ProgramData% or an unsigned exe strongly confirms the backdoor. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15:9443 at the perimeter, and capture the implant binary before deletion (actors delete payloads post-exec). Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for connections to this IP, for cmd.exe children of the implant process, and for SOCKS-proxy listeners; pivot to PsExec/GPO lateral movement noted for The Gentlemen.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15" and RemotePort == 9443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "81.177.215.15" and DestinationPort == 9443
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName=SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  condition: selection

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="81.177.215.15" RemotePort=9443
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="81.177.215.15" All_Traffic.dest_port=9443 by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Kontron ktapi.sys vulnerable driver load (The Gentlemen BYOVD) AIInstallation High
Hunts the load or install of the Kontron ktapi.sys kernel driver that The Gentlemen RaaS weaponised as a zero-day BYOVD to gain kernel R/W and terminate protected Microsoft, ESET, Palo Alto, and SentinelOne security processes. ktapi.sys has no legitimate enterprise footprint, so any load is suspicious. Rationale: ktapi.sys is the specific Kontron driver named in the article and corroborated by Expel as the zero-day BYOVD used to kill Microsoft/ESET/PAN/SentinelOne processes; the driver has effectively zero legitimate presence, making a bare name match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/not-very-gentlemanly-analyzing-a-zero-day-exploit-used-by-the-gentlemen-ransomware-to-disable-targets-edrs/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1547.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kontron industrial/embedded hardware where the vendor API is legitimately installed (rare outside OT/manufacturing)
  • Security researcher detonating the driver in a lab
  • AV/EDR quarantine engine copying the sample (InitiatingProcess would be the security product itself)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe") // exclude EDR quarantine engines copying the sample
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the driver path and the process that wrote/loaded it; check whether the host is genuine Kontron OT hardware (if not, treat as malicious immediately). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, verify EDR/AV agents are still running (BYOVD kills them), and add ktapi.sys to the Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist / WDAC policy. Step 3 (hunt): Look for security-process termination events, subsequent ransomware staging, and the same driver hash across the estate; correlate with The Gentlemen C2 (81.177.215.15) and PsExec/GPO lateral movement.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ktapi.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has "ktapi.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, InstalledBy=SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kontron ktapi.sys Vulnerable Driver Load (The Gentlemen BYOVD)

Citrix Bleed 2 (CVE-2025-5777) exploitation attempts against NetScaler Gateway AIExploitation High
Detects exploitation of CitrixBleed 2 against NetScaler ADC/Gateway — the initial-access vector used by Anubis affiliates. Malformed POST requests to /p/u/doAuthentication.do that omit the passwd parameter and/or carry an oversized attacker-controlled User-Agent trigger the out-of-bounds memory read; high request volume from a single source indicates mass scanning. Rationale: Targets the exact CVE-2025-5777 exploit endpoint /p/u/doAuthentication.do with the documented malformed-POST + oversized-User-Agent signature (per Splunk, GreyNoise and watchTowr analyses), the initial-access method Arctic Wolf attributed to Anubis. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty — NetScaler HTTP telemetry is not shipped to endpoint EDR; this lives in appliance/WAF/proxy logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/citrixbleed-vulnerability-detection-mitigation.html • https://www.greynoise.io/blog/exploitation-citrixbleed-2-cve-2025-5777-before-public-poc • https://labs.watchtowr.com/how-much-more-must-we-bleed-citrix-netscaler-memory-disclosure-citrixbleed-2-cve-2025-5777/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate high-volume authentication bursts from a corporate NAT egress (many users behind one IP)
  • Vulnerability scanners / authorised pentest tooling probing the endpoint
  • Load-balancer health checks hitting the auth endpoint
  • Mobile clients with unusually long but benign User-Agent strings
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm NetScaler build is unpatched for CVE-2025-5777; review the source IP reputation and whether the POSTs lack the passwd parameter or carry an abnormal UA. Step 2 (contain): If exploited, patch/upgrade NetScaler, terminate all active ICA/PCoIP and AAA sessions (kill leaked tokens), and block the source IPs. Step 3 (hunt): Look for post-auth session reuse from new geos/ASNs, follow-on RDP/SMB, PsExec service creation, and RMM tool deployment consistent with the Anubis playbook.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC","Gateway")
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/p/u/doAuthentication.do"
| extend UALen = strlen(RequestClientApplication)
| summarize Requests=count(), MaxUALen=max(UALen), SampleUA=any(RequestClientApplication), Hosts=dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where MaxUALen > 200 or Requests > 50   // oversized UA = leak payload; >50/hr = scanning
| order by Requests desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.dest) as dest from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/p/u/doAuthentication.do*" by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval ua_len=len(http_user_agent) | where ua_len>200 OR count>50 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.dest) as dest from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/p/u/doAuthentication.do*" by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval ua_len=len(http_user_agent) | where ua_len>200 OR count>50 | sort - count
Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) deployment for persistent covert access AICommand & Control Medium
Detects Anubis affiliates configuring a Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) to reach victim environments through an outbound-only encrypted channel that bypasses inbound firewall rules. Flags cloudflared execution with tunnel arguments or trycloudflare tokens, including renamed binaries invoking the tunnel subcommand. Rationale: Article explicitly states select Anubis intrusions 'configure a Cloudflare Tunnel (aka cloudflared)'; matches the cloudflared binary plus the tunnel/token/trycloudflare arguments so renamed binaries invoking the tunnel subcommand are still caught. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Cloudflare Tunnel to expose a local web app
  • IT teams using cloudflared for sanctioned remote access to internal services
  • CI/CD runners establishing ephemeral trycloudflare tunnels for previews
  • Sysadmins testing Cloudflare Zero Trust connectors
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","node.exe") // exclude common developer parents when cloudflared is sanctioned
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine if cloudflared is sanctioned on the host; inspect the tunnel token/config and the parent process (RMM tool or cmd.exe parenting cloudflared is suspicious). Step 2 (contain): Kill the cloudflared process, isolate the host, and block Cloudflare tunnel FQDNs/egress if unauthorised. Step 3 (hunt): Look for co-located RMM tooling, PsExec service creation, credential access, and the Anubis exfil stack (rclone/s5cmd/WinSCP) on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tunnel run","--token ","trycloudflare.com","cloudflared tunnel")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cloudflared.exe"
   or CommandLine has_any ("tunnel run","--token ","trycloudflare.com","cloudflared tunnel")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis defense impairment: Defender RTP disable + SophosUninstall + PCHunter AIInstallation High
Hunts the Anubis pre-encryption defense-evasion cluster: disabling Windows Defender real-time protection via Set-MpPreference/registry, running SophosUninstall, and dropping PCHunter (a kernel process/driver killer). Any one of these in user context is a strong hands-on-keyboard defense-impairment signal. Rationale: Directly encodes the three named Anubis defense-evasion artifacts from the article (Defender real-time protection disablement, SophosUninstall activity, PCHunter-related artifacts); machine accounts excluded to keep FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1089
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Sophos removal during an approved EDR migration
  • IT/helpdesk temporarily disabling Defender RTP for a legit software install or troubleshooting
  • Sysadmin using PCHunter for benign rootkit troubleshooting
  • MDM/RMM tooling toggling Defender settings as part of policy management
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring") // exclude sanctioned MDM policy toggles
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check for a change ticket authorising Defender/Sophos changes; review the initiating process and account — RMM or PsExec parentage plus off-hours timing escalates severity. Step 2 (contain): Re-enable Defender RTP, isolate the host, and preserve PCHunter/driver artifacts; verify no BYOVD driver (ktapi.sys) is loaded. Step 3 (hunt): Look for immediately following shadow-copy deletion, mass file encryption, and the /WIPEMODE encryptor across the estate; confirm which accounts triggered the changes and their lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("PCHunter64.exe","PCHunter.exe","PCHunter32.exe")
   or FileName has "SophosUninstall"
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("PCHunter64.exe","PCHunter.exe","PCHunter32.exe","SophosUninstall")
   or (NewProcessName has "powershell" and CommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
   or CommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anubis Ransomware Defense Impairment Cluster

Anubis exfiltration tooling: rclone/s5cmd/S3 Browser/WinSCP cloud transfer AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Anubis pre-ransomware data-transfer stack — rclone, s5cmd, S3 Browser, WinSCP, and PuTTY/pscp — used to stage and exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled cloud/SFTP storage. Matches the tool binaries plus cloud-copy verbs/remote arguments so renamed rclone/s5cmd builds are still caught. Rationale: Directly lists the exfil tools named in the article (S3 Browser, rclone, s5cmd, WinSCP, PuTTY/pscp) and pairs them with cloud-copy/remote arguments so renamed rclone/s5cmd binaries are still surfaced; kept as hunting tier because these tools have legitimate admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/DevOps teams using rclone or s5cmd for sanctioned S3 sync jobs
  • Admins using WinSCP/PuTTY for routine SFTP file management
  • Data engineers using S3 Browser for legitimate bucket work
  • Scheduled automation copying data to approved cloud storage
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","cloudberry.exe") and FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe")) // exclude sanctioned backup automation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check whether the tool is sanctioned for the host/user and inspect the remote target in the command line — attacker-controlled buckets/SFTP hosts confirm exfil. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block the destination endpoints, and revoke any cloud credentials referenced in configs. Step 3 (hunt): Estimate data staged/transferred (volumes, archive creation), and look for the follow-on Anubis encryptor (/WIPEMODE), Defender disablement, and PsExec lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe","s3browser.exe","winscp.exe","winscp.com","pscp.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rclone ","s5cmd ")
| where FileName in~ ("s3browser.exe","winscp.exe","winscp.com")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy","sync","--config","remote:"," cp "," mb ","cat ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe","s3browser.exe","winscp.exe","winscp.com","pscp.exe")
   or CommandLine has_any ("rclone ","s5cmd ")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("s3browser.exe","winscp.exe") or CommandLine has_any ("copy","sync","--config","remote:"," cp ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis encryptor /WIPEMODE destructive command execution AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of the Anubis ransomware encryptor with its distinctive /WIPEMODE switch, which reduces victim files to 0 KB regardless of ransom payment. Also matches the Anubis flag combination (/KEY /PATH /elevated) used to invoke the encryptor with elevated privileges. Rationale: The /WIPEMODE switch is documented by Rubrik Zero Labs (cited in-article) as the Anubis wiper module that zeroes files to 0 KB — a unique, article-specific command-line token; the /KEY /PATH /elevated combo covers standard encryptor invocation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1485 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software using a coincidentally-named /WIPEMODE or /KEY switch (rare; validate the parent binary)
  • Security team detonating the Anubis sample in a sandbox
  • Red-team ransomware simulation exercise
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): This is near-certainly malicious — confirm the executing binary/hash and whether /WIPEMODE was reached (data destruction imminent/underway). Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from network and storage, kill the process, and trigger the ransomware IR playbook; protect backups/shadow copies from deletion. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same binary hash and command line across all hosts, block lateral movement (PsExec/RDP/SMB), and verify no other systems have staged the encryptor; assess whether /WIPEMODE has already zeroed files for recovery planning.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/WIPEMODE"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "/KEY" and ProcessCommandLine has "/PATH" and ProcessCommandLine has "/elevated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "/WIPEMODE"
   or (CommandLine has "/KEY" and CommandLine has "/PATH" and CommandLine has "/elevated")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-5777")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-5777")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-5777")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.command-and-control

    product: windows

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS infrastructure contact (pamconj.com panel + Cloudflare Worker lure) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Catan and Mouse
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra ID device registration = ARToken PRT persistence after device-code token theft · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ARToken BEC toolkit: inbox forwarding/hiding rule creation on compromised M365 mailbox
ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS infrastructure contact (pamconj.com panel + Cloudflare Worker lure) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network connections to the specific ARToken operator-panel and phishing-lure domains published by Talos (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). A host resolving/connecting to these means a user reached the device-code phishing lure or operator infrastructure — the earliest on-wire signal of this M365 token-theft campaign. Rationale: Uses the three concrete Talos-published IOC domains plus the pamconj.com apex to catch sibling operator subdomains. These are dedicated malicious infrastructure, so any resolution is high-fidelity; cross-checked against Talos, Sekoia and Microsoft reporting of the same EvilTokens/ARToken infra. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/01/eviltokens-device-code-phishing-kit-totally-more-evil-than-we-all-thought/5265409
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating the lure URL in a sandbox/SOAR enrichment from a corporate endpoint
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing to pamconj.com during investigation
  • Web proxy/URL-scanner appliance pre-fetching the domain for categorization
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ appliance logging the blocked query (benign but noisy)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/device and confirm whether the connection was a live browser navigation (device-code lure) vs automated scanner; pull the referring email/Teams message for the same recipient. 2) Contain: block all *.pamconj.com and the workers.dev lure at proxy/DNS; if a real user reached the device-code page, revoke that user's refresh tokens/sessions (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken) and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (new Entra device registration for that user) and UC3 (inbox-rule creation) within 24h; review that user's SigninLogs for device-code grants from unfamiliar IPs.
let ARTokenDomains = dynamic(["dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com","clear90489058903-document.workers.dev","pamconj.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (ARTokenDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let ARTokenDomains = dynamic(["dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com","clear90489058903-document.workers.dev","pamconj.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (ARTokenDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
