Entra ID device registration = ARToken PRT persistence after device-code token theft AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens persistence step: after stealing a refresh token via device-code phishing, the operator registers a new device in Entra ID to obtain a Primary Refresh Token for durable SSO that survives password resets. Surfaces device add/register/join audit events with the acting user, source IP and target device for rapid correlation to a suspicious sign-in. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'Primary Refresh Token (PRT) persistence' capability and corroborated by Sekoia/Microsoft describing refresh-token-driven device registration in Entra ID. Device add/register audit operations are the concrete, queryable footprint of that step; Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because Entra ID audit isn't in FDR or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/microsoft-365-phishing-panel-uses-oauth-device-code-flow/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user enrolling a new phone/laptop into Intune/Entra (BYOD or refresh cycle)
  • Autopilot/Intune bulk device provisioning by IT during onboarding
  • Windows Hello for Business device registration on password change
  • Service desk registering a replacement device for a user
Suppression filter
| where ActorIp !in ("<intune_provisioning_egress_ip>")  // NOTE: replace only if you maintain a known Intune egress allowlist; otherwise correlate ActorIp against SigninLogs device-code/foreign-IP sign-ins
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each registration confirm the actor UPN, source IP and device name; check whether the user's most recent sign-in was a device-code grant or came from an unfamiliar/foreign IP within the prior hour. 2) Contain: if unattributable, disable/remove the newly registered device, revoke the user's refresh tokens and PRTs (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken + session invalidation), and require MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: enumerate all devices registered by the same actor IP across the tenant, review SharePoint/OneDrive mass-download and inbox-rule creation (UC3) for the affected mailbox.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device","Register device","Add device")
| extend Ip = tostring(IPAddress)
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Ip, CountryCode, City, ObjectName, ObjectType
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device","Register device","Add device","Update device")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend TargetDevice = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, TargetDevice, Result, ResultReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken BEC toolkit: inbox forwarding/hiding rule creation on compromised M365 mailbox AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens post-compromise BEC action: automated creation of inbox rules that forward/redirect mail externally and delete or move messages to hide attacker activity. Targets mailbox audit events for New/Set-InboxRule carrying forwarding or delete/move parameters. Rationale: Directly targets ARToken's documented BEC capability ('inbox rule creation for forwarding and deleting messages') via the exact Exchange audit operations and forwarding/delete parameters. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because M365 mailbox audit isn't shipped to those platforms in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberscoop.com/artoken-bec-platform-cisco-talos/ • https://gbhackers.com/eviltokens-linked-artoken-panel/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately setting up out-of-office/auto-forward to a personal or delegate mailbox
  • Admin-configured transport/journaling rule mistaken for a user inbox rule
  • Power-user creating a 'move to folder' organization rule for newsletters
  • Migration tooling recreating rules during a mailbox move
Suppression filter
| where Params !has "@yourcorpdomain.com"  // keep only rules forwarding/redirecting OUTSIDE the org; internal delegate forwarding is common and low-risk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the rule forwards/redirects to an EXTERNAL domain or deletes/moves security-alert mail; check the ClientIP/country against the user's normal sign-in pattern and recent device-code sign-ins. 2) Contain: delete the malicious rule, revoke the user's tokens and PRTs, reset credentials, and block the external forwarding destination at the mail gateway. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (infra contact) and UC2 (new device registration) for the same user; search for identical rule names/forwarding targets across other mailboxes to scope the BEC blast radius.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where RawEventData has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Params = tostring(Parameters)
| where Params has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Params, OfficeWorkload
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

union
    ( ImFileEvent

Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] INTERPOL law-enforcement lure delivering ransomware via Proton Drive archive · [LLM] Platform-aware phishing: Ninite Loader delivering ConnectWise/Itarian RAT on Windows · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: AI Compute Hijacking, Apple Email Flaw, BlueHammer Ransomware + 14 S
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BeepRAT (DCRat variant) delivered as HFY.exe telephone-management .NET app from archive · [LLM] BeepRAT scheduled-task persistence created by HFY.exe loader · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BeepRAT DoH-based C2 resolution and api.service.bio beacon · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
BeepRAT (DCRat variant) delivered as HFY.exe telephone-management .NET app from archive AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of HFY.exe, the .NET 'phone number management' decoy that Rubrik Zero Labs attributes to the China-nexus BeepRAT multi-stage loader, especially when launched from an archive-extraction path (Downloads/Temp) alongside database-driver DLLs. Article-specific because HFY.exe is the named first-stage binary of this campaign. Rationale: HFY.exe is the specifically-named .NET decoy binary from Rubrik Zero Labs; pairing it with archive-extraction parent processes/paths distinguishes the BeepRAT infection from any unrelated file of the same short name. Cross-checked against: • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate in-house or third-party utility genuinely named HFY.exe run by a user
  • IT deploying a benign telephony/PBX management tool from a Downloads folder
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox host onboarded to the tenant
  • Software-packaging team staging installers under \Temp\ that include an unrelated HFY.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ProgramData\\Package Cache","\\Program Files\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and check it against Rubrik's BeepRAT sample and VT/ThreatFox; inspect sibling files in the same folder for database-driver DLLs bundled with the ZIP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the HFY.exe process tree, and quarantine the extraction directory. 3) Hunt: on the same device look for a new scheduled task (UC2), DoH lookups / api.service.bio beacons (UC3), and in-memory .NET assembly loads; sweep the org for the same SHA256 and archive filename.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HFY.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Desktop\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","winrar.exe","7zg.exe","7zfm.exe","7z.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\HFY.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BeepRAT HFY.exe Telephone-Management Decoy Execution
id: 6f2b1c8a-2d4e-4a71-9f3c-7b1e0a9c4d21
description: Detects execution of HFY.exe, the .NET first-stage decoy used by the BeepRAT/DCRat variant reported by Rubrik Zero Labs.
references:

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="HFY.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\$$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
BeepRAT scheduled-task persistence created by HFY.exe loader AIInstallation Medium
Hunts schtasks.exe /create (or a scheduled-task registration) whose parent is the BeepRAT decoy HFY.exe or a binary running from an archive-extraction path — the persistence mechanism Rubrik documented for this China-nexus RAT. Article-specific via the HFY.exe parent pivot rather than a generic schtasks alert. Rationale: The article states BeepRAT 'establishes persistence on the host via scheduled tasks'; anchoring the schtasks /create on the HFY.exe parent (or archive-path executable parent) keeps this specific to the campaign instead of a generic scheduled-task rule. Cross-checked against: • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign app legitimately named HFY.exe that registers an updater scheduled task
  • Portable software run from Downloads that self-registers a maintenance task
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample generating expected persistence
  • An installer temporarily extracted to \Temp\ that creates a first-run task
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks command line to capture the task name, trigger, and the executable it points to; verify the pointed-to binary hash. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, isolate the host, and kill HFY.exe. 3) Hunt: confirm the HFY.exe drop (UC1) and outbound DoH/api.service.bio beacon (UC3); search other hosts for a scheduled task pointing at the same payload path or referencing the same task name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HFY.exe"
   or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\") and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create"
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\HFY.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BeepRAT Scheduled Task Persistence via HFY.exe
id: a1c9e77f-3b52-4d0a-8e11-2f6c4b9d5e30
description: Detects schtasks.exe /create spawned by the BeepRAT decoy HFY.exe, the persistence step reported by Rubrik Zero Labs.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:*create* @ParentImage:(*\HFY.exe OR *\hfy.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/HFY\.exe$/i
| regex("/create", field=CommandLine)

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" Processes.parent_process_name="HFY.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" Processes.parent_process_name="HFY.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
BeepRAT DoH-based C2 resolution and api.service.bio beacon AICommand & Control High
Hunts the BeepRAT command-and-control channel: direct contact with the C2 domain api.service.bio, or the HFY.exe loader issuing DNS-over-HTTPS lookups to public DoH resolvers to covertly resolve its C2 (as Rubrik documented). Article-specific via the exact C2 domain plus the non-browser DoH pivot. Rationale: api.service.bio is the article/Rubrik-linked C2 domain (highest-fidelity IOC); the DoH-resolver clause catches the documented DNS-over-HTTPS resolution when the domain itself is hidden from plaintext DNS. Note: because BeepRAT uses DoH, plaintext DNS logs may not show api.service.bio — the DeviceNetworkEvents/DoH-provider path covers that gap. Cross-checked against: • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app coincidentally resolving api.service.bio if the domain is ever repurposed
  • A non-browser enterprise app configured to use DoH resolvers for privacy
  • Security tooling / EDR that itself performs DoH lookups
  • A user-installed DoH proxy (e.g. a privacy client) generating resolver traffic
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedgewebview2.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and confirm whether it is HFY.exe or an unsigned/.NET binary; capture the resolved IP behind api.service.bio. 2) Contain: block api.service.bio and the resolved C2 IP at egress, isolate the host, and kill the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 IP across all hosts, correlate with HFY.exe execution (UC1) and scheduled-task persistence (UC2), and review for data staging preceding exfil since BeepRAT lacks egress restrictions.
let DoHResolvers = dynamic(["cloudflare-dns.com","mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com","chrome.cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","doh.opendns.com","dns.quad9.net","doh.cleanbrowsing.org"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "api.service.bio"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HFY.exe" and RemoteUrl in~ (DoHResolvers))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname =~ "api.service.bio" or Url has "api.service.bio"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INTERPOL law-enforcement lure delivering ransomware via Proton Drive archive AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails impersonating INTERPOL / law-enforcement 'investigation' notices that direct recipients to a Proton Drive URL hosting a password-protected archive, the delivery chain Bitdefender tied to a custom ransomware payload targeting SMBs. Article-specific via the law-enforcement lure + Proton Drive hosting combination. Rationale: Combines Bitdefender's specifics — impersonation of law enforcement (INTERPOL) as the lure and Proton Drive (drive.proton.me) as the delivery host for a password-protected archive — a pairing distinctive to this campaign. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon left empty because the detection is bound to Defender EmailEvents+EmailUrlInfo mailflow telemetry with no clean equivalent on those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business partner genuinely sharing a file via Proton Drive to an inbox
  • Internal compliance/legal team circulating a real investigation notice with an 'evidence' subject
  • Privacy-conscious users who routinely receive Proton Drive share links
  • Newsletter or press email discussing an INTERPOL operation matching the subject keywords
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the sender domain/SPF-DKIM-DMARC on AuthenticationDetails and open the Proton Drive URL in a sandbox to capture the hosted archive and password. 2) Contain: purge the message from all recipient mailboxes (soft-delete/ZAP), block the sender and the specific Proton Drive share URL, and warn recipients not to open it. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents for anyone who clicked, then correlate to endpoint archive extraction and subsequent mass file-encryption / ransom-note activity on those users' devices.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where UrlDomain has "proton"
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("drive.proton.me","proton.me") or Url has "drive.proton.me"
| where Subject has_any ("INTERPOL","Interpol","investigation","law enforcement","police","evidence","suspicious activity","criminal")
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject,
          Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where UrlDomain has "proton"
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ ("drive.proton.me","proton.me") or Url has "drive.proton.me"
| where Subject has_any ("INTERPOL","Interpol","investigation","law enforcement","police","evidence","suspicious activity","criminal")
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject,
          Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where Email.direction="inbound" (Email.subject="*INTERPOL*" OR Email.subject="*investigation*" OR Email.subject="*law enforcement*" OR Email.subject="*suspicious*activity*" OR Email.subject="*evidence*") by Email.src_user Email.recipient Email.subject Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email where Email.direction="inbound" (Email.subject="*INTERPOL*" OR Email.subject="*investigation*" OR Email.subject="*law enforcement*" OR Email.subject="*suspicious*activity*" OR Email.subject="*evidence*") by Email.src_user Email.recipient Email.subject Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Platform-aware phishing: Ninite Loader delivering ConnectWise/Itarian RAT on Windows AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Cofense-reported chain where a fingerprinted Windows victim receives Ninite Loader, which then installs the trusted-but-abused ConnectWise ScreenConnect client (or Itarian RAT) as a remote-access trojan — flagged when the RMM/loader is spawned by a browser or from a download path. Article-specific via the Ninite Loader → ConnectWise/Itarian pivot. Rationale: Uses Cofense's named tools — Ninite Loader as the delivery loader and ConnectWise ScreenConnect / Itarian RAT as the repurposed remote-access payloads — constrained to a browser/loader parent so it catches phishing-driven RMM installs rather than sanctioned deployments. Kept hunting-tier because ConnectWise is dual-use. Cross-checked against: • https://cofense.com/blog/the-platform-you-trust-is-the-platform-they-target • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/phishing-campaigns-auto-adapt-victims-device-os • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying ConnectWise ScreenConnect for remote support
  • A user intentionally downloading the real Ninite installer from ninite.com to install apps
  • An MSP-managed endpoint where ScreenConnect is the sanctioned RMM
  • A pentest/red-team engagement using ScreenConnect as an approved C2/RMM
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("relay.screenconnect.com/e=Support") and DeviceName in~ ("HELPDESK-RMM-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether ScreenConnect/Itarian is a sanctioned RMM for this host; inspect the ScreenConnect relay/instance ID in the command line and compare to your approved tenant. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, uninstall/kill the ScreenConnect client and Ninite Loader, and block the attacker relay domain. 3) Hunt: review the preceding browser download URL for the fingerprinting landing page, check macOS/Android users hitting the same URL for credential-harvest redirects, and sweep for the same relay instance ID across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ConnectWise"
         or FileName has "ScreenConnect"
         or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect","connectwisecontrol.com","relay.screenconnect.com","Itarian","itarian.com")
         or FileName has_any ("Ninite","Itarian"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Ninite.exe","explorer.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","Ninite","Itarian") or CommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect","connectwisecontrol.com","relay.screenconnect.com","itarian.com")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Ninite.exe","explorer.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Ninite Loader Spawning ConnectWise/Itarian RAT via Browser (Cofense Platform-Aware Phishing)

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="Ninite.exe" OR Processes.process="*ScreenConnect*" OR Processes.process="*connectwisecontrol*" OR Processes.process="*Itarian*") Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Ninite.exe","explorer.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="Ninite.exe" OR Processes.process="*ScreenConnect*" OR Processes.process="*connectwisecontrol*" OR Processes.process="*Itarian*") Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Ninite.exe","explorer.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

| where Account !endswith "$"

ConsentFix and ClickFix: How Microsoft 365 Accounts are Hijacked in 3 Seconds

BleepingComputer
2026-07-02 15 use cases 6 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

ConsentFix and ClickFix attacks steal Microsoft 365 tokens in seconds using fake prompts and OAuth flows. Learn how these MFA bypass tactics work and how to defend against them. [...]

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1190 T1204.004 T1486 T1528 T1566
Domainssecurity-updater.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ConsentFix lure delivery: inbound email link to DocSend/Dropbox or ConsentFix phishing infra · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ConsentFix: interactive browser sign-in to Azure CLI / dev-tool first-party app · [LLM] ClickFix: PowerShell/mshta download-execute spawned from Run dialog (explorer parent) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ConsentFix: Azure CLI token redemption from divergent IP within 10 min of interactive sign-in · [LLM] Post-session-theft mailbox abuse: auto-forwarding / inbox rule creation via stolen M365 session · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ConsentFix: interactive browser sign-in to Azure CLI / dev-tool first-party app AIExploitation High
Hunts the core ConsentFix token-theft primitive: a normal user completing an interactive browser OAuth sign-in to Azure CLI (or Azure PowerShell / VS Code / Visual Studio / Teams PowerShell) first-party apps. These developer tooling apps are near-never used interactively via a browser by regular staff, so the event is the fingerprint of the localhost-callback consent lure described in the article. Rationale: Uses the concrete first-party ApplicationIds confirmed by Push Security / Mitiga / gblock as the apps ConsentFix abuses (Azure CLI 04b07795-... is a public client, so the auth code alone yields tokens). Interactive browser sign-in to CLI/dev tooling by ordinary users is the high-fidelity anomaly. Localhost callback mechanic cross-checked against the consentfix-phishing-page screenshot and Push Security write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/consentfix-oauth-phishing-explained-how-token-based-attacks-bypass-mfa-in-microsoft-entra-id • https://www.gblock.app/articles/consentfix-v3-azure-cli-oauth-microsoft-365-phishing • https://detection.fyi/elastic/detection-rules/integrations/azure/initial_access_entra_id_oauth_phishing_via_first_party_microsoft_application/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or cloud/DevOps engineer legitimately running `az login` with the interactive browser flow
  • IT admin authenticating to Azure PowerShell via browser during troubleshooting
  • VS Code Azure extension sign-in by a developer
  • GitHub Codespaces / Cloud Shell auth redeeming codes for a genuine user
  • First-time Azure onboarding session for a new cloud engineer
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("devbox","jumpbox") and AccountUpn has_any ("svc-","admin-"))   // exclude known dev/admin workstations after per-tenant tuning
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the signed-in user is in a role that legitimately uses Azure CLI/PowerShell (DevOps, cloud eng). Check IPAddress/Location/UserAgent against the user's baseline and whether a localhost callback error immediately preceded on the endpoint. Step 2 (contain): If unexpected, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset and re-MFA, and review/remove any app consents granted. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on AccountObjectId for a non-interactive token redemption from a different IP within 10 minutes (UC2), and check for new mailbox forwarding/inbox rules and Graph enumeration from the same session.
let VulnerableFirstPartyApps = dynamic(["04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56","04f0c124-f2bc-4f59-8241-bf6df9866bbd","12128f48-ec9e-42f0-b203-ea49fb6af367"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId in (VulnerableFirstPartyApps)   // Azure CLI + dev-tool public clients abused by ConsentFix
| where IsInteractive == true
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ClientAppUsed == "Browser"                    // interactive browser flow = the lure, not native CLI use
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, Browser, DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
let VulnerableFirstPartyApps = dynamic(["04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56","04f0c124-f2bc-4f59-8241-bf6df9866bbd","12128f48-ec9e-42f0-b203-ea49fb6af367"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId in (VulnerableFirstPartyApps)
| where IsInteractive == true
| where ResultType == 0
| where ClientAppUsed == "Browser"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ConsentFix: Azure CLI token redemption from divergent IP within 10 min of interactive sign-in AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the two sign-in events ConsentFix produces for a single OAuth authorization-code theft: the victim's interactive sign-in to a dev-tool first-party app, followed by a non-interactive token redemption for the same user/app from a different IP within ~10 minutes. Human-delayed, geographically-dispersed redemption distinguishes the attack from legitimate CLI use (same IP, seconds). Rationale: Directly encodes Push Security's ConsentFix detection: two sign-ins sharing UserId+AppId, second within ~10 min, divergent IPs (legitimate CLI redeems within seconds from the same IP). App IDs and the 10-minute/divergent-IP heuristic are corroborated across Push Security and gblock write-ups. Datadog query is the base scope; IP-divergence + 10-min grouping is set at rule level. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.gblock.app/articles/consentfix-v3-azure-cli-oauth-microsoft-365-phishing • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/consentfix-oauth-phishing-explained-how-token-based-attacks-bypass-mfa-in-microsoft-entra-id
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Roaming/VPN user whose interactive login and token redemption egress via different IPs
  • Mobile hotspot failover changing the source IP between sign-in and token refresh
  • CI/CD or automation redeeming an Azure CLI code from a build agent for a legitimate service context
  • Corporate proxy pool assigning different egress IPs to auth vs Graph calls
  • Legitimate cross-region Azure Cloud Shell usage by a developer
Suppression filter
| where RedeemCountry != VictimCountry or DelaySec > 30   // suppress same-country sub-30s redemptions typical of legit CLI/Cloud Shell
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Compare VictimIP vs RedeemIP geolocation/ASN and DelaySec; a >30s delay with a foreign or hosting-provider ASN redemption is high-signal. Confirm the user is not a routine CLI user. Step 2 (contain): Immediately revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens for the AccountObjectId, block the RedeemIP, and disable the account pending review. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all activity from the attacker session (mailbox reads, new inbox/forwarding rules, added app consents, Graph directory enumeration) and sweep other users for interactive sign-ins to the same AppScope.
let AppScope = dynamic(["04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56","04f0c124-f2bc-4f59-8241-bf6df9866bbd","12128f48-ec9e-42f0-b203-ea49fb6af367"]);
let Interactive = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ApplicationId in (AppScope)
    | where IsInteractive == true and ErrorCode == 0
    | project VictimTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, ApplicationId, VictimIP = IPAddress, VictimCountry = Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId in (AppScope)
| where IsInteractive == false and ErrorCode == 0
| project RedeemTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, ApplicationId, RedeemIP = IPAddress, RedeemCountry = Country, RedeemUserAgent = UserAgent
| join kind=inner Interactive on AccountObjectId, ApplicationId
| where RedeemTime between (VictimTime .. VictimTime + 10m)   // 10-min human-delayed redemption window (Push Security)
| where RedeemIP != VictimIP                                  // attacker infra differs from victim device
| project VictimTime, RedeemTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', RedeemTime, VictimTime), AccountUpn, ApplicationId, VictimIP, VictimCountry, RedeemIP, RedeemCountry, RedeemUserAgent
| order by VictimTime desc
let AppScope = dynamic(["04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56","04f0c124-f2bc-4f59-8241-bf6df9866bbd","12128f48-ec9e-42f0-b203-ea49fb6af367"]);
let Interactive = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where AppId in (AppScope)
    | where IsInteractive == true and ResultType == 0
    | project VictimTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, UserPrincipalName, AppId, VictimIP = IPAddress, VictimLoc = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion);
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId in (AppScope)
| where ResultType == 0
| project RedeemTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, AppId, RedeemIP = IPAddress, RedeemUA = UserAgent
| join kind=inner Interactive on UserId, AppId
| where RedeemTime between (VictimTime .. VictimTime + 10m)   // 10-min human-delayed redemption window
| where RedeemIP != VictimIP
| project VictimTime, RedeemTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', RedeemTime, VictimTime), UserPrincipalName, AppId, VictimIP, VictimLoc, RedeemIP, RedeemUA
| order by VictimTime desc

ClickFix: PowerShell/mshta download-execute spawned from Run dialog (explorer parent) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the ClickFix execution step where the victim pastes an attacker command into the Windows Run dialog after a fake CAPTCHA/verification prompt, causing PowerShell, mshta, cmd or curl to launch as a child of explorer.exe with download-and-execute arguments. Targets the article's explicit recommendation to detect 'unusual PowerShell activity originating from normal user processes.' Rationale: ClickFix pastes the payload into the Win+R Run dialog, so the interpreter's parent is explorer.exe (not Office, which is separately covered). Pairing that parent anomaly with download-execute cmdline tokens is the article's named signal ('unusual PowerShell from normal user processes') and avoids the excluded Office-spawns-script / encoded-PowerShell rules. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/consentfix-and-clickfix-how-microsoft-365-accounts-are-hijacked-in-3-seconds/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1204 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually pasting an Invoke-WebRequest one-liner into Run for legitimate tooling install
  • Software deployment scripts triggered via a Run-dialog shortcut
  • Developer using curl.exe from Run to test an endpoint
  • Help-desk remote-guidance walking a user through a PowerShell command
  • Legitimate .hta-based internal application launched by double-click
Suppression filter
| where not(AccountName in~ ("admin","helpdesk") and DeviceName has_any ("IT-","ADMIN-"))   // suppress known admin build/support hosts after tuning
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and resolve the URL/host it fetches; check if the user reported a CAPTCHA/'verify you are human' prompt just prior. Inspect any child process and dropped file (SHA256). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the endpoint, kill the process tree, and block the fetched domain/IP at proxy/EDR. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host and user for follow-on stager execution, new persistence (Run keys/scheduled tasks), and — critically — subsequent interactive Azure CLI sign-ins (UC1) indicating the ClickFix chained into ConsentFix.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"   // Win+R Run dialog / double-click origin
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("iwr","invoke-webrequest","iex","invoke-expression","downloadstring","downloadfile","mshta http","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","-nop","frombase64string",".hta","curl ","certutil","start-bitstransfer","http://","https://")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("iwr","invoke-webrequest","iex","downloadstring","downloadfile","mshta http","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","-nop","frombase64string",".hta","curl ","certutil","http://","https://")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Run-Dialog Download-Execute via Explorer-Spawned Interpreter

      - 'http'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.exe OR *\\EXPLORER.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\curl.exe) @CommandLine:(*iwr* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *IEX* OR *DownloadString* OR *"mshta http"* OR *"-w hidden"* OR *FromBase64String* OR *.hta* OR *certutil* OR *http*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|mshta|cmd|curl|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(iwr|invoke-webrequest|iex|downloadstring|downloadfile|mshta http|-w hidden|-windowstyle hidden|frombase64string|\\.hta|certutil|https?://)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

ConsentFix lure delivery: inbound email link to DocSend/Dropbox or ConsentFix phishing infra AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ConsentFix delivery stage: inbound, delivered email carrying a link to DocSend/Dropbox (often password-protected to evade inspection) or to the campaign's phishing infrastructure. Surfaces the lure before the victim reaches the fake Microsoft sign-in page. Rationale: Article names Dropbox/DocSend as the trusted-platform delivery channel (often password-protected); Push Security supplies corroborated ConsentFix payload domains (trustpointassurance.com, fastwaycheck.com, previewcentral.com) which I use as high-fidelity infra IOCs, plus the article's security-updater.com. Generic Dropbox/DocSend is tiered hunting due to legitimate-use noise; the infra-domain lookups are alert-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/consentfix-and-clickfix-how-microsoft-365-accounts-are-hijacked-in-3-seconds/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate business use of DocSend for sales/investor documents
  • Genuine Dropbox file-share links between partners
  • Marketing or vendor newsletters linking to Dropbox-hosted assets
  • Password-protected but benign contract shares from a real counterparty
  • Internal team sharing large files via a Dropbox link
Suppression filter
| where not(SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("docsend.com","dropbox.com") and Verdict == "trusted-service-lure")   // drop platform-native notification mails; keep third-party-sent links
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For ConsentFix-infra hits, treat as confirmed-bad and identify all recipients; for DocSend/Dropbox hits, check sender reputation, SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails, and whether the landing page renders a Microsoft sign-in. Step 2 (contain): Soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide (ZAP), block the infra domains at mail/proxy, and warn recipients not to interact. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate recipients against UrlClickEvents and subsequent interactive Azure CLI sign-ins (UC1) and ClickFix executions (UC3) to find anyone who progressed past delivery.
let LureDomains = dynamic(["docsend.com","dropbox.com","dropboxusercontent.com"]);
let ConsentFixInfra = dynamic(["trustpointassurance.com","fastwaycheck.com","previewcentral.com","security-updater.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain has_any (LureDomains) or UrlDomain has_any (ConsentFixInfra)
| extend Verdict = iff(UrlDomain has_any (ConsentFixInfra), "ConsentFix-infra", "trusted-service-lure")
| project Timestamp, Verdict, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
let ConsentFixInfra = dynamic(["docsend.com","trustpointassurance.com","fastwaycheck.com","previewcentral.com","security-updater.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (ConsentFixInfra)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-session-theft mailbox abuse: auto-forwarding / inbox rule creation via stolen M365 session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the actions-on-objective stage after ConsentFix session theft: the attacker uses the stolen token (no password, MFA bypassed) to create mailbox forwarding or inbox rules that exfiltrate or hide mail. Targets the article's stated impact — 'session access to email' — and the hidden-rule tradecraft typical of OAuth-token account takeover. Rationale: The article's stated impact is session access to email; token-theft account takeovers routinely pivot to auto-forwarding/hiding rules. Keys on Exchange audit operations (New-InboxRule/Set-Mailbox) with forwarding/deletion parameters — high-fidelity when the initiating IP/UserAgent diverges from the user's baseline (pairs with UC1/UC2). Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/consentfix-oauth-phishing-explained-how-token-based-attacks-bypass-mfa-in-microsoft-entra-id
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately setting up out-of-office forwarding to a delegate
  • Admin configuring a mailbox forward during offboarding
  • Power user creating an inbox rule to file newsletters into a folder
  • Migration tooling adjusting mailbox delivery settings
  • Executive assistant setting redirect rules on a shared mailbox
Suppression filter
and RawEventData has_any ("ForwardTo","RedirectTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo") and RawEventData !has "@yourtenantdomain.com"   // keep only rules forwarding OUTSIDE the org (replace yourtenantdomain.com per tenant)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the rule's target — external ForwardTo/RedirectTo addresses or DeleteMessage on security-sender mail is high-signal; compare ClientIP/UserAgent to the user's baseline and to any UC1/UC2 anomalous Azure CLI sign-in. Step 2 (contain): Disable/remove the rule, revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens, and block the external forward address. Step 3 (hunt): Review the mailbox for read/exfil activity, other tenant users with new forwarding rules in the same window, and OAuth app consents granted from the same session.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Set-Mailbox","New-TransportRule")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeliverToMailboxAndForward","DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, Application, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Set-Mailbox","New-TransportRule")
| where Parameters has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeliverToMailboxAndForward","DeleteMessage")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, OriginatingServer, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc
