level: high
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 16 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actor known as ToddyCat has been attributed to a new malware called Umbrij that's designed to gain surreptitious access to a victim's email correspondence via the Google API. "In this campaign, the attackers focused their attention on corporate email communications hosted on Gmail, targeting access compromise via APIs," Kaspersky said in a detailed report published this week. "

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading via signed BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop · [LLM] Scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR ('KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp') · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Headless Chromium remote-debugging launched against copied BackupFiles profile (STRD) · [LLM] Google OAuth endpoint reached by browser spawned from Umbrij side-load binary
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Browser credential store copied into %LOCALAPPDATA% BackupFiles staging directory · [LLM] OAuth grant / API access to 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' app (Umbrij token abuse) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading via signed BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop AIInstallation High
Hunts the specific DLL side-loading chain ToddyCat uses to launch the Umbrij .NET stealer: three legitimate signed binaries each insecurely loading a named rogue DLL. Article-specific because it pairs each abused host binary with its exact malicious module name and hash rather than generic side-loading. Rationale: Uses the exact abused host binaries (BDSubWiz.exe/VSTestVideoRecorder.exe/GoogleDesktop.exe), their paired rogue DLL names, the Umbrij DLL MD5s (28cb7b26.../bae82a15.../9f5f2f0f...), and the anomalous drop paths confirmed by Securelist. The binary+DLL pairing is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/ • https://cyberpress.org/toddycat-automates-gmail-compromise/
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by anomalous-path filter)
  • Genuine Visual Studio test agent running VSTestVideoRecorder.exe from the VS install tree
  • A developer manually placing a signed tool in C:\Users\Public for testing
  • Security tooling copying signed binaries to Temp during sandbox detonation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files\Bitdefender" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading binary runs from Temp/Vss/Public and the loaded DLL name/hash matches (log.dll, GoogleServices.dll, or the VideoRecorderEngine DLL). Pull the DLL and check signer/ConfuserEx obfuscation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the side-loading process, quarantine the rogue DLL and the co-located signed EXE. 3) Hunt: search the same host and user for the scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp', a %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\BackupFiles directory, and headless-browser remote-debugging launches (UC3/UC4).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "BDSubWiz.exe" and FileName =~ "log.dll")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
    or MD5 in~ ("28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1","bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66","9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedDllPath = FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel has no native image-load table; pivot on the host binary executing from an anomalous location (Umbrij drop paths)
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\Vss\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR ('KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp') AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/execution primitive Umbrij used: a scheduled task named after Kaspersky's EDR agent that launches the digitally signed side-loading binary. Article-specific because it keys on the exact impersonated task name Kaspersky reported during its threat hunt. Rationale: Keys on the exact impersonated task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' reported by Kaspersky; a scheduled task with that name not created by a genuine Kaspersky process is an unambiguous ToddyCat indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kaspersky Endpoint Security installer/updater registering its own EDR task (excluded by initiating-process filter)
  • Backup/imaging tools cloning a host that legitimately runs Kaspersky and replaying task XML
  • Sysadmin manually re-creating a Kaspersky task after repair
  • SCCM/Intune redeploying Kaspersky agent
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Kaspersky Lab\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the task action/XML — confirm it launches a signed binary (BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop) from Temp/Vss/Public rather than the real Kaspersky path, and identify the creating process. 2) Contain: delete the rogue task, isolate the host, quarantine the referenced binary+DLL. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (side-load), and check for BackupFiles browser-profile copies and headless remote-debugging launches on the same host/user.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
| where AdditionalFields has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" or ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("avp.exe","kavfsslp.exe")   // exclude genuine Kaspersky-created tasks
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698   // scheduled task created
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Headless Chromium remote-debugging launched against copied BackupFiles profile (STRD) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the core Shadow Token via Remote Debug (STRD) step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge headless with a remote debugging port pointed at a copied user profile in BackupFiles to hijack the live Gmail session. Article-specific via the exact flag+path combination. Rationale: Combines the exact Chromium flag (--remote-debugging-port) with the article's attacker-specific staging folder 'BackupFiles'; no legitimate workflow launches a browser headless-debugging against a copied BackupFiles profile. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://gbhackers.com/toddycat-uses-shadow-token/
ATT&CKT1185 T1550.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright automated UI test suites launching headless Chrome with remote-debugging (won't reference BackupFiles)
  • Selenium/browser-automation CI runners on developer endpoints
  • Manual developer debugging with --remote-debugging-port against a normal profile path
  • Enterprise screenshot/monitoring tools driving Chrome headless
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm --user-data-dir points into a BackupFiles folder and identify the parent process (expect a side-load binary). Grep the host for the Umbrij log file containing an OAuth authorization code. 2) Contain: kill the browser+parent, isolate host, and initiate Google Workspace token revocation for the affected user. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC5 (OAuth network flow) and UC6 (Google Workspace Migration/Sync app grant) for the same user, and revoke sessions in Google Admin.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser credential store copied into %LOCALAPPDATA% BackupFiles staging directory AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Umbrij's profile-theft step: copying Login Data, Web Data, cookies and Local/IndexedDB storage of each authenticated profile into a BackupFiles directory under the Chrome/Edge app-data path. Article-specific via the exact folder and the named profile artifacts. Rationale: Keys on the exact attacker-created 'BackupFiles' subfolder under the Chrome/Edge LocalAppData path plus the named profile artifacts (Login Data, Web Data, cookies, IndexedDB); browsers never write those files into a BackupFiles directory, and the non-browser initiating process makes it high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/migration utility that literally names its folder 'BackupFiles' and copies browser profiles (rare; verify initiating process)
  • Browser profile-migration tools during OS upgrade
  • IT-driven roaming-profile sync copying Login Data
  • User manually backing up a browser profile into a folder coincidentally named BackupFiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","browsermigration.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process that wrote into BackupFiles (expect a side-load binary, not chrome/msedge) and enumerate which profiles/emails were staged. 2) Contain: isolate host, remove the BackupFiles directory after forensic capture, and force-reset the affected user's browser sessions and Google Workspace tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC3 headless remote-debug launch and UC6 Google Workspace app grant on the same user; assume cookie/session theft and rotate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "BackupFiles"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data For Account","Web Data","Preferences","Secure Preferences","Cookies") or FolderPath has_any ("IndexedDB","Local Storage","Network")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "BackupFiles"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Login Data","Web Data","Preferences","Secure Preferences","IndexedDB","Local Storage","Network","Cookies")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google OAuth endpoint reached by browser spawned from Umbrij side-load binary AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the STRD token-acquisition network step: a Chrome/Edge process spawned by one of the abused side-load host binaries contacts accounts.google.com / oauth2.googleapis.com to drive the OAuth consent-and-token flow. Article-specific via the parent-process chain, not generic Google traffic. Rationale: The fidelity comes from the parent chain — a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/VSTestVideoRecorder/GoogleDesktop hitting Google OAuth endpoints — plus the specific client project IDs 279448736670/1095133494869 (Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Outlook) in the proxy URL where available; plain accounts.google.com traffic alone is filtered out by the parent predicate. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://cyberpress.org/toddycat-automates-gmail-compromise/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal user browsing to accounts.google.com (excluded — requires side-load parent or remote-debugging flag)
  • Legit Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Outlook actually deployed and used by the org (validate at myaccount.google.com/connections)
  • Browser automation frameworks authenticating to Google
  • Enterprise SSO flows to oauth2.googleapis.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "BackupFiles" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser's parent is a side-load host binary (or the remote-debugging flag is present) and capture the full OAuth URL/client_id from proxy logs. 2) Contain: isolate host, and in Google Admin revoke the 'Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Microsoft Outlook' authorization and force token/session invalidation for the user. 3) Hunt: search UC6 for subsequent Gmail/Drive/Contacts API access via that app, and check the Umbrij log file for the exfiltrated authorization code.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("accounts.google.com","oauth2.googleapis.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires web-proxy telemetry that captures the full OAuth request URL/query
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "accounts.google.com/o/oauth2" or Url has "oauth2.googleapis.com"
| where Url has_any ("279448736670","1095133494869")   // Google Workspace Migration / Sync for Outlook client project IDs
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MSEdge.exe)) (@DestinationHostname:accounts.google.com OR @DestinationHostname:oauth2.googleapis.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest

| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ParentBaseFileName=/\\?(BDSubWiz|VSTestVideoRecorder|GoogleDesktop)\.exe$/i | ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge)\.exe$/i}, field=[ContextProcessId], key=[TargetProcessId], include=[ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
OAuth grant / API access to 'Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook' app (Umbrij token abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the objective of the STRD attack: an OAuth authorization and subsequent Gmail/Drive/Contacts API access via the Google Workspace Migration or Sync for Microsoft Outlook application, whose client IDs Umbrij drives to mint tokens. Article-specific via the exact abused app names and client project IDs. Rationale: Uses the exact application names ('Google Workspace Migration/Sync for Microsoft Outlook') Kaspersky told defenders to look for at myaccount.google.com/connections, plus the corroborated client project IDs 279448736670/1095133494869; token grants to these apps in an org that doesn't use them are a direct Umbrij indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/toddycat-linked-umbrij-malware-abuses.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Org genuinely migrating mailboxes from Exchange/Outlook into Google Workspace (validate with IT — legitimate Migration tool use)
  • Users who legitimately run Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook
  • Admin-approved third-party marketplace OAuth apps with similar scopes
  • A one-off sanctioned data-import project
Response runbook
1) Triage: at myaccount.google.com/connections (or Google Admin > Security > API controls) confirm whether the Migration/Sync app is sanctioned; review IP/geo/user-agent and the granted Gmail/Drive/Contacts/Calendar scopes. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke the app's access to invalidate all issued OAuth tokens and force-reauth the user. 3) Hunt: enumerate all users who granted the same app, review Gmail API read volume (users.messages.list/get) for bulk export, and correlate to the endpoint chain (UC1–UC5).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or ObjectName has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or AdditionalFields has_any ("279448736670","1095133494869")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, Application, ActionType, ActivityType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ObjectName, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or ObjectName has_any ("Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook","Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook")
    or AdditionalFields has_any ("279448736670","1095133494869")
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, Application, ActionType, ActivityType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ObjectName, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound exploitation of Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF (CVE-2026-20230) from campaign infra · [LLM] Cisco Unified CM SSRF file:// arbitrary file-write payload (CVE-2026-20230)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue Apache Axis AdminService / JSP webshell on Cisco Unified CM (CVE-2026-20230 post-exploit)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Inbound exploitation of Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF (CVE-2026-20230) from campaign infra AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Cisco Unified CM WebDialer service that carry SSRF exploit markers (file://, Apache Axis AdminService) or originate from the Defused-reported campaign IP 156.146.38.167. This is the initial-access step Cisco confirmed is under active exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploit chain (WebDialer service + Apache Axis AdminService + file:// SSRF) confirmed by Cisco's advisory, SOCRadar and DarkReading; the campaign IP 156.146.38.167 is currently single-source (Defused) so it is used as a booster, not the sole anchor. Defender/Falcon left empty because CUCM is a Linux Tomcat appliance not onboarded to EDR — detection lives on the wire (CEF) and in appliance syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/less-than-24-hours-attackers-weaponize-cisco-cucm-flaw
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDialer click-to-call SOAP traffic from internal CTI/UC applications (will lack file:// and AdminService markers)
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing the WebDialer endpoint from a known scan subnet
  • Internal penetration-test or Cisco TAC-guided validation of the patch from a corporate source IP
  • Security-team replaying the public PoC from a sanctioned research host
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has "webdialer" and not (RequestURL has_any ("file://","file:/","AdminService","/axis/")) and SourceIP !in (CampaignIPs))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a Unified CM host and inspect the full RequestURL for a file:// scheme or Axis AdminService call; check whether WebDialer is enabled and whether the CUCM version predates 14SU6/15SU5. 2) Contain: block SourceIP 156.146.38.167 at the perimeter, disable the WebDialer service (Cisco's interim mitigation), and restrict WebDialer to trusted management networks. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same DestinationIP for follow-on /axis/ AdminService requests and newly created .jsp files under the Tomcat web root (see webshell UC), and review CUCM install/security logs for unexpected files.
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["156.146.38.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "webdialer"
| where SourceIP in (CampaignIPs)
   or RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file:/", "AdminService", "/axis/", "%2Ffile", "%66%69%6c%65")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Unified CM SSRF file:// arbitrary file-write payload (CVE-2026-20230) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to a Unified CM host whose URI/query embeds a file:// scheme, the mechanism Defused observed attackers using to write attacker-controlled files onto the appliance via the WebDialer SSRF. Content-pivot detection independent of source IP. Rationale: Uses the article's specific technique string 'properly constructed file:// payloads to create files' plus the corroborated Axis/WebDialer target paths; matches on request content so it fires regardless of rotating source IPs. URL-encoded variants included because SSRF payloads are commonly percent-encoded to bypass filters. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW
ATT&CKT1190 T1105
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners injecting file:// test strings during authorized SSRF assessments
  • WAF/IPS logging the raw payload of a blocked request (verify DeviceAction shows block, not allow)
  • Developers or Cisco TAC reproducing the PoC in a lab that shares the SIEM
  • Legitimate application passing a file: parameter unrelated to CUCM (excluded by the webdialer/axis/ccmadmin path requirement)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","drop","reset")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the file:// path in RequestURL to see what the attacker attempted to read/write, and confirm whether the WAF allowed or blocked (DeviceAction). 2) Contain: if allowed, isolate the CUCM host from untrusted networks, disable WebDialer, and snapshot the appliance for forensics before patching to 14SU6/15SU5. 3) Hunt: search the same host for follow-on /axis/services/AdminService calls and newly written .jsp files, and review CUCM audit logs for unexpected OS-level files created around the request timestamp.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("webdialer", "/axis/", "/ccmadmin/")
| where RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file:%2F%2F", "file:/", "%66%69%6c%65%3a")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue Apache Axis AdminService / JSP webshell on Cisco Unified CM (CVE-2026-20230 post-exploit) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-SSRF stage where attackers invoke the Apache Axis AdminService on the CUCM Tomcat stack to deploy a rogue SOAP service and then access an attacker-dropped .jsp webshell in the web root — the code-execution/persistence tail of the CVE-2026-20230 chain. Rationale: Targets the corroborated post-exploit chain (SOCRadar/DarkReading: rogue Apache Axis service deployed via AdminService, then a JSP file-writer/command shell in the Tomcat web dir). AdminService invocation and new .jsp access on a production CUCM are highly abnormal, giving a sharp signal distinct from the initial SSRF request. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/less-than-24-hours-attackers-weaponize-cisco-cucm-flaw • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco built-in .jsp application pages accessed during normal CCMAdmin/Self-Care usage (baseline the specific known .jsp set)
  • Cisco upgrade/COP file installation touching Tomcat webapps
  • Authorized admin using legitimate Axis-based CUCM management functions from a management host
  • Vulnerability scanner fingerprinting the /axis/ path
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL contains ".jsp" and DestinationHostName !has "cucm" and RequestURL !has "AdminService")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact .jsp path and whether it exists in a stock CUCM image; a non-catalog .jsp or any external-sourced GET/POST to /axis/services/AdminService is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the CUCM host, capture the .jsp and Tomcat logs, and treat the appliance as root-compromised — plan rebuild/restore rather than in-place cleanup. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the originating SSRF file:// request and source IP, review outbound connections from the CUCM host for C2/reverse shell, and check for credential/config exfiltration and lateral movement from the appliance.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/axis/services/AdminService", "AdminService", "/axis/services")
   or (RequestURL contains ".jsp" and RequestURL has_any ("/webdialer/", "/axis/", "/ccmadmin/", "/cucm-uds/"))
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20230")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20230")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) via /api/v1/validate/code POST AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the Langflow code-validation endpoint that CVE-2025-3248 abuses for unauthenticated Python execution, the exact entry vector JADEPUFFER used. Article-specific because it pins the named CVE's documented vulnerable endpoint on an internet-facing Langflow box rather than a generic web exploit. Rationale: Pins CVE-2025-3248's documented vulnerable endpoint (/api/v1/validate/code) + POST, the exact unauthenticated-RCE path the article names as JADEPUFFER's way in. Defender left empty because MDE does not ingest reverse-proxy/web access logs; endpoint manifestation is covered by the execution UC. WebSearch was blocked in this session so no external corroboration could be pulled.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow flow authors saving/validating custom Python components
  • Internal CI/CD or health-check jobs POSTing to the validate endpoint
  • Security scanners / ASM tools probing the known CVE path
  • Blue-team CVE-2025-3248 validation testing
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "HealthCheck" and SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body/user-agent and source IP; confirm whether the payload contains exec/import/os/subprocess and whether the Langflow build is <1.3.0 (still vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the Langflow instance off the public internet, and rotate every API key/cloud credential reachable from its environment. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a child shell/interpreter spawned by uvicorn/gunicorn/python, beacons to 45.131.66.106, and new cron persistence.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/validate/code"   // CVE-2025-3248 Langflow code-exec endpoint
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow web service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python) spawning shell or download tool AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the Langflow RCE: the web-service process spawning a shell, curl, or wget to run recon and sweep secrets (MinIO minioadmin default, cloud keys) and reach the staging server 64.20.53.230. Article-specific because a Langflow/uvicorn parent spawning /bin/sh is the RCE payload firing, not normal app behaviour. Rationale: A public-facing Langflow/uvicorn process spawning /bin/sh or curl is the RCE detonating; enriched with the article's concrete secret-sweep artifacts (minioadmin default cred, staging IP 64.20.53.230, cloud-provider key names). WebSearch blocked so no second-source confirmation; grounded in article body.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom components that legitimately shell out to system tools
  • In-container entrypoint scripts where python/uvicorn launches a shell at startup
  • Ops using curl/wget from an app-service context for package or model downloads
  • Health-check or exporter sidecars spawning shell probes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint.sh","docker-entrypoint") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for recon (id, uname, env), credential paths (.aws/credentials, minioadmin), or egress to 64.20.53.230. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Langflow process tree, and rotate all secrets that lived in that environment (OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepSeek/Gemini keys, AWS/Azure/GCP/Alibaba/Tencent creds). 3) Hunt: pivot to network events for 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230, and check for a new cron job beaconing every 30 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| extend SecretSweep = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws","OPENAI","ANTHROPIC","DEEPSEEK")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| extend SecretSweep = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SecretSweep
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any connection to the JADEPUFFER command-and-control IP 45.131.66.106, the target of a /beacon check-in on port 4444 every 30 minutes. Article-specific: a dedicated, published malicious IP + port + URI from Sysdig's IOC list. Rationale: 45.131.66.106 is Sysdig's published JADEPUFFER C2 IP with a documented :4444/beacon check-in every 30 minutes; a dedicated malicious IP makes any hit high-fidelity. WebSearch was blocked so the IOC is taken directly from the article's Sysdig indicator list without independent second-source confirmation.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation infrastructure deliberately touching the IOC
  • Blue-team IOC-validation connectivity tests
  • A benign service that later gets assigned the same recycled VPS IP (verify timeframe)
  • Security scanner sweeping the /24 that includes this IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process/context making the connection (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether check-ins recur near a 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: block 45.131.66.106 (and staging 64.20.53.230) egress at perimeter, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: on that host enumerate cron/systemd timers, look for the Langflow RCE parent-child chain, and check MySQL/Nacos hosts for README_RANSOM tables and dropped databases.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence mechanism: a scheduled job (cron/crond/atd) launching curl/wget/shell that contacts 45.131.66.106, the article's 'scheduled task that pinged the attacker's server every 30 minutes.' Distinct from the raw network IOC because it pivots on the scheduler parent, catching the persistence even if the beacon lands intermittently. Rationale: Combines the article's 30-minute scheduled-task persistence with the concrete C2 IP 45.131.66.106, pivoting on the cron parent so the persistence is caught even between beacon hits. WebSearch blocked; IOC and behaviour taken from the article/Sysdig indicators only.
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned monitoring cron jobs that curl an external endpoint (verify the IP)
  • Admin-authored heartbeat scripts to a legitimate host that shares the /24
  • Backup/telemetry agents scheduled via cron reaching out on interval
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the cron entry (crontab -l, /etc/cron.d/*, /var/spool/cron) and confirm the target IP and 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron/systemd unit, block 45.131.66.106 egress, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to the Langflow RCE process chain and to any MySQL/Nacos host showing README_RANSOM or dropped tables; check for a MinIO server still on minioadmin default creds.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","atd")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","atd")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nacos auth bypass (CVE-2021-29441) via 'User-Agent: Nacos-Server' to create rogue admin AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to Nacos user-management endpoints carrying the User-Agent 'Nacos-Server' identity that CVE-2021-29441 abuses to bypass authentication and add an admin account, exactly what JADEPUFFER did before encrypting the config store. Article-specific: named CVE + Nacos default-signing-key takeover leading to a planted admin. Rationale: Uses CVE-2021-29441's well-known bypass signature — the spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent hitting /nacos/v1/auth/users to add an admin — which the article names as JADEPUFFER's Nacos takeover step. Defender/Falcon/Datadog empty because this is a web-request artifact those EDR/FDR feeds don't carry. WebSearch was blocked, so no external corroboration was obtained.
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nacos cluster nodes using the Nacos-Server identity for inter-node calls (baseline internal peer IPs)
  • Security testing of the Nacos CVE by the blue team
  • Misconfigured client library that copies the Nacos-Server user-agent
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/non-cluster and check whether a new Nacos user/admin was created around that time. 2) Contain: take Nacos off the public internet, rotate the default signing key, remove rogue admin accounts, and stop it connecting to its DB as root. 3) Hunt: check the backing MySQL for a README_RANSOM table and dropped tables, and correlate with the Langflow RCE host and C2 45.131.66.106.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestClientApplication has "Nacos-Server"   // CVE-2021-29441 identity-bypass User-Agent
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/v1/auth/users"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on JADEPUFFER's impact stage — creation of the README_RANSOM ransom table, presence of the ransom Bitcoin address / Proton contact, or a root-context mysql client issuing DROP TABLE/DROP DATABASE after the Nacos config store was encrypted. Article-specific via three unique published strings. Rationale: Three unique published IOCs — ransom table README_RANSOM, Bitcoin address 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy, contact e78393397@proton.me — plus root-context mysql DROP make this near-zero-FP and specific to the JADEPUFFER impact stage. WebSearch was blocked so these strings are taken from the article's Sysdig indicator list without a second source.
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA restoring/testing on a lab copy who names a table README_RANSOM while investigating the IOC
  • Threat-hunt queries themselves logging the IOC strings into command lines
  • Legitimate scheduled DROP TABLE cleanup jobs (verify not root-from-internet and no ransom strings)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threat-hunt" and AccountName != "dba-restore-svc"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the README_RANSOM table / note and whether DROP/TRUNCATE ran under the DB root account; identify the source session and host. 2) Contain: isolate the DB server, revoke internet exposure of the DB admin account, and preserve logs — note the actor claims AES but printed the key once and never saved it, so recovery from backups is the only path. 3) Hunt: trace back to the Nacos auth-bypass and Langflow RCE hosts, block C2 45.131.66.106 and staging 64.20.53.230, and audit MinIO for the minioadmin default login.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (FileName in~ ("mysql","mysqladmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DROP TABLE","DROP DATABASE","TRUNCATE"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (SyslogMessage has_all ("DROP","TABLE") and SyslogMessage has "root")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
