PoC script executed from clone/Downloads/Temp within 2 min of git clone AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the ChocoPoC infection habit: a researcher clones a fake PoC repo then runs python/powershell against EXPLOIT_POC.py (or poc/exploit .py) from a Downloads, Temp or /tmp clone path seconds later — the moment the compiled loader triggers. Rationale: Anchors on the article's EXPLOIT_POC.py trigger-file name plus the clone-and-run researcher behavior described as the infection route; the git-clone→python within 120s window strips generic PoC testing noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1204.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate red-teamer safely running a clean community PoC in a lab VM
  • CI pipeline that clones a repo and runs its poc.py test harness
  • Researcher re-running a previously vetted exploit.py from Downloads
  • Automated malware-analysis harness detonating PoCs by design
Suppression filter
| where CloneCmd has_any ("github.com","gitlab.com") and DelaySec <= 120
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the CloneCmd URL — is the source repo a brand-new/unknown GitHub account tied to a hot CVE? Check whether skytext/frint were installed on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, snapshot for forensics, and rotate any credentials that lived on it. 3) Hunt: check the host for gradient.pyd/.so (UC2), outbound to 91.132.163.78 (UC4), and Mapbox/DoH beaconing by python (UC6).
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSec = 120;
let GitClones = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName in~ ("git.exe","git") and ProcessCommandLine has "clone"
    | project GitTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, CloneCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python","powershell.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("EXPLOIT_POC","exploit.py","poc.py")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/Downloads/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner GitClones on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (GitTime .. GitTime + WindowSec*1s)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, CloneCmd, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, GitTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 120s;
let GitClones = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has "git" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "clone"
    | project GitTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CloneCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","powershell")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("EXPLOIT_POC","exploit.py","poc.py")
| join kind=inner GitClones on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (GitTime .. GitTime + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, CloneCmd, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, GitTime)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*EXPLOIT_POC* OR *exploit.py* OR *poc.py*) @process.command_line:(*python* OR */tmp/* OR *Downloads*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\powershell.exe) @CommandLine:(*EXPLOIT_POC* OR *exploit.py* OR *poc.py*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(python3?|powershell)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/(EXPLOIT_POC|exploit\.py|poc\.py)/i
| CommandLine=/(Downloads|Temp|\/tmp\/)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3","python","powershell.exe")) (Processes.process IN ("*EXPLOIT_POC*","*exploit.py*","*poc.py*")) (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Downloads\\*","*\\Temp\\*","*/tmp/*","*/Downloads/*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3","python","powershell.exe")) (Processes.process IN ("*EXPLOIT_POC*","*exploit.py*","*poc.py*")) (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Downloads\\*","*\\Temp\\*","*/tmp/*","*/Downloads/*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Outbound connection to ChocoPoC exfiltration server 91.132.163.78 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host connecting to the ChocoPoC large-upload/exfiltration server 91.132.163.78. This is the out-of-band channel the RAT uses for bulk file/folder uploads, separate from its Mapbox dead-drop control channel. Rationale: 91.132.163.78 is the single hard IOC IP named in the article for large uploads and is confirmed still-live by CyberSecurityNews; a static IP match has near-zero ambiguity. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox intentionally connecting to the IOC to validate it is live
  • A researcher's automated IOC-reachability sweep
  • Coincidental reuse of the same hosting IP by an unrelated benign service after takedown
  • Security scanner reaching the IP as part of an internet-wide scan
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — python/gradient indicates confirmed ChocoPoC exfil; note bytes_out to gauge data loss. 2) Contain: block 91.132.163.78 at egress, isolate the host, and preserve netflow/pcap. 3) Hunt: on the same host confirm skytext/frint install (UC1), gradient loader (UC2), and browser/SSH credential access (UC5); assume any credentials/reports on the host are exfiltrated and rotate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "91.132.163.78"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "91.132.163.78"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python process reading browser credential stores and SSH/cloud secrets AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ChocoPoC stealer behavior: a python-hosted process reading Chrome/Brave/Edge/Firefox login/cookie databases plus ~/.ssh and ~/.aws secrets. Ties the RAT's credential harvesting to its Python execution context. Rationale: Article states ChocoPoC pulls saved passwords/cookies/history from Chrome, Brave, Edge and Firefox and grabs local databases and shell/network config; scoping the browser secret-store and ~/.ssh|~/.aws reads to a python initiator ties the theft to the RAT's Python runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://cyberpress.org/chocopoc-targets-python-dependencies/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.001 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate python browser-automation (Selenium profile handling) touching Login Data
  • A credential-harvesting security tool the researcher runs on purpose (e.g. a browser-cred audit script)
  • Backup software written in python snapshotting the user profile
  • Python dotfile/SSH management tooling reading ~/.ssh/config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("selenium","playwright") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("selenium","playwright"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the python command line and parent — is it tied to a freshly cloned PoC or skytext/gradient? Legit automation usually runs from a known project path. 2) Contain: isolate the host and immediately rotate browser-saved passwords, session cookies, SSH keys and cloud (AWS) credentials for that user. 3) Hunt: correlate with outbound to 91.132.163.78 (UC4) and Mapbox/DoH beaconing (UC6) to confirm exfiltration; expand credential rotation to any client/engagement secrets stored on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python")
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data","id_rsa","credentials"))

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath

Python beaconing to Mapbox dead-drop / DoH resolvers (ChocoPoC C2) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts ChocoPoC's covert control channel: a python-hosted process resolving/contacting Mapbox and DNS-over-HTTPS resolver endpoints, which the RAT abuses as a domain-fronted dead drop for its orders. Rationale: Article specifies the RAT reads orders from a Mapbox dataset used as a dead drop, resolving it over DNS-over-HTTPS with a domain-fronting trick; scoping Mapbox/DoH-resolver contact to a python initiator surfaces that channel while excluding normal browser Mapbox usage. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1102 T1090.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A python GIS/mapping app legitimately calling the Mapbox API
  • A python tool configured to use DoH (cloudflare-dns.com / dns.google) for privacy
  • Data-science notebooks fetching Mapbox tiles
  • Corporate DoH-based DNS client written in python
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("geopandas","folium","mapbox","rasterio"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating python has no legitimate mapping/GIS purpose and correlate timing with a recent PoC clone or skytext install. 2) Contain: isolate the host; block the offending Mapbox dataset/DoH endpoint at egress if not business-required. 3) Hunt: pivot to bulk uploads to 91.132.163.78 (UC4) and credential store access (UC5); pull the Mapbox account/dataset id from proxy logs for takedown reporting. Sentinel note: DoH/Mapbox is high-FP without process context (ImDnsActivity lacks initiator), so treat as a fleet-wide hunt not an alert.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.mapbox.com","mapbox.com","cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com","doh.opendns.com")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.mapbox.com","mapbox.com","cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","doh.opendns.com")
| summarize QueryCount = count(), Queries = make_set(DnsQuery, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe) @DestinationHostname:(*mapbox.com* OR *cloudflare-dns.com* OR *dns.google* OR *doh.opendns.com*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/(python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| DomainName=/(mapbox\.com|cloudflare-dns\.com|dns\.google|doh\.opendns\.com)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*api.mapbox.com*","*mapbox.com*","*cloudflare-dns.com*","*dns.google*","*doh.opendns.com*")) by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*api.mapbox.com*","*mapbox.com*","*cloudflare-dns.com*","*dns.google*","*doh.opendns.com*")) by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-64446", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-14847", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-10520", "CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-48908")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-64446", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-14847", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-10520", "CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-48908")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

            - '\mshta.exe'

SharePoint RCE CVE-2026-45659 Added to CISA KEV After Active Exploitation

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a high-severity flaw impacting Microsoft SharePoint Server to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-45659 (CVSS score: 8.8), is a case of remote code execution arising from the deserialization of untrusted data. The issue

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Attacker remote-access channels: cloudflared tunnel, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH tunnel

SharePoint/Triofox LFI probing for win.ini & web.config (Storm-2603 initial access) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to internet-facing SharePoint/Gladinet Triofox endpoints that retrieve win.ini or web.config (including the corroborated /storage/t.dn LFI endpoint used to steal the ASP.NET machineKey). This is the article's stated initial-access probe preceding CVE-2025-11371 / CVE-2026-45659 exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact LFI artifacts (win.ini, web.config) plus the second-source Huntress-confirmed /storage/t.dn and UploadDownloadProxy Triofox endpoints; retrieval of web.config yields the machineKey enabling ViewState RCE, so a served (status<400) hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/gladinet-centrestack-triofox-local-file-inclusion-flaw • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/from-lfi-to-rce-active-exploitation.html • https://securityaffairs.com/183259/hacking/cve-2025-11371-unpatched-zero-day-in-gladinet-centrestack-triofox-under-attack.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing for LFI as part of authorized assessments
  • Legitimate SharePoint health-check tooling reading web.config over HTTP
  • Backup/config-management agents fetching web.config via web endpoints
  • Security researchers or red-team engagements hitting /storage/t.dn
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "nmap", "masscan", "Nuclei") and cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8")   // exclude sanctioned scanners / internal ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP and confirm whether web.config/machineKey content was actually returned (status 200 + response size); check if the source IP is an internal scanner or external. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and, if a served web.config is confirmed, rotate the SharePoint/Triofox ASP.NET machineKey and force IIS recycle to invalidate forged ViewState. 3) Hunt: on the affected server look for follow-on ViewState deserialization POSTs, w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell, and any Velociraptor or remote-access-tool execution within the following hours.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem has_any ("win.ini", "web.config", "t.dn") or csUriQuery has_any ("win.ini", "web.config")
| where scStatus < 400   // only successful/served retrievals of the sensitive file
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Velociraptor DFIR agent executed as attacker tooling (Storm-2603 execution) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution or service install of the Velociraptor DFIR binary on hosts that are not sanctioned incident-response endpoints. The article states Storm-2603 deployed Velociraptor with SYSTEM privileges to blend malicious activity with trusted admin behaviour. Rationale: Velociraptor is named explicitly in the article as the DFIR tool Storm-2603 abused; the binary name, client artifact strings, and SYSTEM-integrity execution are distinctive and rare outside sanctioned IR, giving low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/velociraptor-incident-response-tool-abused-for-remote-access • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
ATT&CKT1105 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Your own DFIR/IR team legitimately deploying Velociraptor during an investigation
  • MSSP or Sophos/Huntress-managed Velociraptor agent as a sanctioned monitoring tool
  • Security lab / detection-engineering testing of Velociraptor
  • Threat-hunting exercises running the binary on a jump-host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("IR-JUMPHOST01", "DFIR-TOOLS01")   // populate with sanctioned IR endpoints
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a sanctioned IR endpoint and whether your team deployed Velociraptor; inspect the config/frontend URL in the command line to see where it reports (attacker C2 vs internal). 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host, kill the Velociraptor process/service, and capture the config file for the C2 address. 3) Hunt: pivot on the config's frontend domain across DeviceNetworkEvents, and look for co-occurring new admin accounts, cloudflared tunnels, and NSecKrnl.sys driver drops on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "velociraptor.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("velociraptor", "artifact_collector", "Velociraptor.Client", "--config", "frontend")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Velociraptor"
// exclude sanctioned DFIR jump-hosts by DeviceName if you have them
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\velociraptor.exe" or CommandLine has_any ("velociraptor", "artifact_collector", "Velociraptor.Client")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

NSecKrnl.sys vulnerable driver drop/install (Storm-2603 BYOVD EDR tampering) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation on disk or service installation of the vulnerable NSecKrnl.sys driver, which the article states was used as a BYOVD conduit to tamper with endpoint protection and reduce visibility. Any appearance of this driver name is high-signal. Rationale: NSecKrnl.sys is the exact vulnerable driver named in the article as the BYOVD conduit for EDR tampering; a fixed, uncommon driver filename makes any hit essentially a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188359/unpatched-sharepoint-servers-opened-the-door-to-multiple-attackers-microsoft-finds.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate product that genuinely ships a driver literally named NSecKrnl.sys (verify vendor signature and path)
  • Security-research/malware-analysis sandbox intentionally detonating the BYOVD sample
  • Restore of a forensic image that contains the artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path, SHA256 and signer of NSecKrnl.sys and the process that wrote it (InitiatingProcessFileName); check whether a matching kernel service was registered (7045). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, block the driver hash org-wide, and treat EDR telemetry from that host as untrusted (assume tampering) — validate the sensor is still reporting. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same driver hash/name and service, and correlate with Velociraptor execution, new admin accounts, and EDR sensor-stop/config-change events around the same timestamp.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NSecKrnl.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceFileName has "NSecKrnl" or ServiceName has "NSecKrnl"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker remote-access channels: cloudflared tunnel, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH tunnel AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts execution of the three specific redundant remote-access channels the article attributes to Storm-2603 for persistent C2: Cloudflare tunneling (cloudflared tunnel), Zoho Assist agents, and Visual Studio Code SSH/remote tunnels. Targets server assets where these tools are not normally present. Rationale: The three channels (Cloudflare tunneling, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH) are named verbatim in the article and confirmed by second sources; scoping cloudflared/code to the 'tunnel' subcommand keeps the signal on the actual tunnel behaviour rather than benign launches. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/ • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately running 'code tunnel' (VS Code Remote Tunnels) on workstations
  • IT support using Zoho Assist as a sanctioned remote-support tool
  • Sanctioned Cloudflare Tunnel deployment for internal app publishing
  • CI/CD or dev machines with cloudflared for local testing
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "DEV" and DeviceName !has "WKS"   // reduce developer-workstation noise; keep server/DC assets in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the host is a server/DC (high suspicion) vs a developer workstation, and inspect the tunnel target — cloudflared config/token, Zoho session ID, or VS Code tunnel name — for external ownership. 2) Contain: on server/infrastructure assets, kill the process and any associated service, and block the tunnel egress domains (*.trycloudflare.com, *.cloudflare.com tunnels, zoho assist domains) from that host. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/account with Velociraptor, NSecKrnl.sys, and new admin-account creation, and check whether the same remote-access tooling appears on a second organization/host (article notes lateral movement into a second org).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe", "ZA_Connect.exe", "ZMAgent.exe", "ZohoMeeting.exe", "ZohoURS.exe")
    or (FileName =~ "code.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\cloudflared.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel")
    or NewProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access.exe", "ZA_Connect.exe", "ZMAgent.exe", "ZohoMeeting.exe", "ZohoURS.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\code.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Redundant Remote-Access Tunnels (cloudflared / Zoho Assist / VS Code SSH)
id: 9e2b6f04-1c8a-47d3-b5e9-6a4f2d7c3b11
description: Detects Storm-2603 persistent remote-access channels - Cloudflare tunnel, Zoho Assist agents, and VS Code remote/SSH tunnel - on Windows hosts.
references:

  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\cloudflared.exe OR *\\Cloudflared.exe) AND @CommandLine:*tunnel*) OR @Image:(*\\ZA_Access.exe OR *\\ZA_Connect.exe OR *\\ZMAgent.exe OR *\\ZohoMeeting.exe OR *\\ZohoURS.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\code.exe OR *\\Code.exe) AND @CommandLine:*tunnel*))

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

New local/domain admin account creation and privileged-group grant (Storm-2603 persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts creation of new accounts followed by (or directly) their addition to Administrators / Domain Admins / Enterprise Admins, and command-line net user/group /add of admin members. The article states Storm-2603 escalated by creating new local and domain administrator accounts. Rationale: Directly targets the article's 'created new local and domain administrator accounts' behaviour via both auth telemetry (4728/4732 to well-known admin SID S-1-5-32-544) and the net.exe /add command line, which is the concrete on-host method. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188359/unpatched-sharepoint-servers-opened-the-door-to-multiple-attackers-microsoft-finds.html
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1136.002 T1078.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT provisioning of new admin accounts during onboarding/imaging
  • Identity-management/PAM automation adding accounts to privileged groups
  • Legitimate helpdesk scripts using net localgroup administrators /add
  • Domain migration or M&A activity creating admin accounts in bulk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-idm", "svc-provisioning") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pam_agent.exe")   // exclude sanctioned provisioning identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the actor (SubjectUserName/InitiatingProcessAccountName) and the created account; confirm whether a change ticket exists and whether the actor is itself a recently-created or compromised account. 2) Contain: disable the newly created account, remove it from privileged groups, and force a password reset on the actor account; on a DC, verify replication of the malicious group change is reversed. 3) Hunt: correlate the new account's first logons across hosts (lateral movement to a second org per the article), and check for co-occurring Velociraptor, cloudflared/Zoho/VS Code tunnels, and NSecKrnl.sys on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.exe", "net1.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/add"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "user") or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("localgroup", "group") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("administrators", "domain admins", "enterprise admins"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4728, 4732)   // member added to global (4728) / local (4732) security-enabled group
| where TargetSid == "S-1-5-32-544" or TargetUserName in~ ("Administrators", "Domain Admins", "Enterprise Admins")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Actor = SubjectUserName, AddedMember = MemberName, Group = TargetUserName, EventID
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2025-11371")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2025-11371")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Unpatched Argo CD Repo-Server Flaw Could Let Attackers Take Over Kubernetes Clusters

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Argo CD, a widely used tool for deploying software to Kubernetes, has an unpatched flaw in its repo-server component that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code, provided they can reach the component's internal network port. Synacktiv, which found the bug, says it can lead to a full cluster takeover. There is no fix and no CVE. The firm says it reported the flaw to Argo CD's maintainers in

Argo CD repo-server exploit: kustomize --helm-command points to non-helm script AIExploitation High
Hunts the Synacktiv unauthenticated RCE against Argo CD repo-server, where an attacker sets kustomize's --helm-command to an attacker-supplied script (pulled from a rogue Git repo) instead of the helm binary. Fires when a kustomize process runs with --helm-command whose target does not resolve to helm. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit primitive — kustomize's --helm-command re-pointed away from the helm binary. Cross-checked with Synacktiv reporting relayed via The Hacker News; legitimate kustomize-with-helm always calls a path ending in 'helm', so a non-helm target is high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/kustomize/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom kustomize helm plugin wrapper script that ends in something other than 'helm' (e.g. a vendored 'helm-wrapper.sh')
  • In-house CI that shims helm via a shell script for private OCI auth
  • Config Management Plugin (CMP) that legitimately templates via a custom binary
  • Debugging/troubleshooting by a platform engineer manually running kustomize with a custom helm path
Suppression filter
| where HelmCmd !in~ ("/custom/bin/helm-wrapper.sh") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the value of --helm-command; confirm whether the target is an approved helm binary path or an unexpected script/temp path. Identify the host — it should be an argocd-repo-server pod/node. 2) Contain: cordon the node, kill the repo-server pod, and apply the Argo CD network policies (networkPolicy.create=true) so only Argo CD components can reach repo-server (TCP 8081) and Redis (6379). Rotate the Redis password. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents from repo-server for egress to attacker Git/registry, check Redis 'mfst' cache integrity, and audit recently synced Applications for attacker-supplied workloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| extend HelmCmd = extract(@"--helm-command[=\s]+([^\s]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(HelmCmd)
| where HelmCmd !endswith "helm" and HelmCmd !endswith "helm.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, HelmCmd, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| extend HelmCmd = extract(@"--helm-command[=\s]+([^\s]+)", 1, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(HelmCmd) and HelmCmd !endswith "helm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, HelmCmd, TargetProcessCommandLine
title: Argo CD Kustomize helm-command Points to Non-Helm Payload

description: Detects kustomize invoked with --helm-command whose target is a shell/script path rather than helm, matching the Synacktiv Argo CD repo-server RCE.

Argo CD repo-server / kustomize spawning shell or network tooling AIExploitation High
Detects code execution on the Argo CD repo-server: the parent process argocd-repo-server or kustomize spawning an interactive shell or network utility (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python). This is the observable outcome of the --helm-command RCE where an attacker-controlled script runs in place of helm. Rationale: The repo-server normally only execs git, helm, kustomize and gpg; a shell or curl/wget/nc child is the direct execution artifact of the article's script-injection RCE. Parent-child pairing keeps this far tighter than a bare LOLBin hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/security/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom Config Management Plugins that legitimately shell out to curl/python for private repo auth
  • Init scripts or entrypoint wrappers baked into a custom repo-server image
  • Helm hooks or pre-render scripts that fetch dependency charts via curl/wget
  • Platform-engineer debugging inside the repo-server pod via kubectl exec (would show sh/bash)
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "registry-1.docker.io")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; confirm it is not a known CMP or debugging session (correlate with kubectl exec / DeviceLogonEvents). 2) Contain: kill the repo-server pod, enable Argo CD network policies, and block the repo-server pod's egress to any non-Git/non-Redis destination. 3) Hunt: pivot to the destination IP/URL of any curl/wget, check for a subsequent Redis connection and cache 'mfst' modification, and review new Applications synced after the event.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Argo CD service account deploys privileged / host-escape workload AIInstallation High
Detects the cluster-takeover payload: after poisoning the Argo CD Redis cache, the Argo CD service account syncs a workload whose pod spec requests privileged mode, hostPID/hostNetwork/hostIPC, or a hostPath mount of the Docker/container socket. Targets the Kubernetes API audit trail of the malicious manifest being applied. Rationale: Ties the article's outcome ('Argo CD deployed an attacker-supplied workload') to the concrete host-escape primitives (privileged, hostPID, docker.sock) that a takeover payload needs, scoped to the Argo CD service account as the requestor so normal privileged system pods don't match. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1610 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate privileged DaemonSets (CNI, CSI, node-exporter, Falco) that Argo CD genuinely manages via GitOps
  • A platform team intentionally deploying a privileged monitoring agent through Argo CD
  • hostNetwork ingress controllers deployed by Argo CD
  • Cluster bootstrap/app-of-apps sync that includes system components with hostPath mounts
Suppression filter
| where Namespace !in ("kube-system","monitoring","argocd") and not (Name has_any ("cni","csi","node-exporter","falco","ingress"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the offending manifest against the Git source of truth — if the privileged spec is not in the declared repo, it is Redis cache poisoning. Confirm the source Application and repoURL. 2) Contain: pause auto-sync on the affected Application, delete the malicious workload, rotate the Redis password, and enable network policies isolating repo-server/Redis. 3) Hunt: enumerate all pods created by the argocd SA in the window, check for reverse shells / crypto miners in those pods, and validate no ClusterRoleBinding was added for the argocd SA.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets")
| extend Requestor = tostring(Username)
| where Requestor has "argocd"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ('"privileged":true','"hostPID":true','"hostNetwork":true','"hostIPC":true','/var/run/docker.sock','/var/run/crio/crio.sock','"hostPath"')
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor, Verb, Res, Namespace=tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestUri

source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(pods OR deployments OR daemonsets OR statefulsets) @user.username:*argocd* (@requestObject.spec.hostPID:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostNetwork:true OR @requestObject.spec.volumes.hostPath.path:\/var\/run\/docker.sock OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets") "user.username"="*argocd*" | spath | search ("requestObject.spec.hostPID"=true OR "requestObject.spec.hostNetwork"=true OR "requestObject.spec.hostIPC"=true OR "requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.privileged"=true OR "requestObject.spec.template.spec.containers{}.securityContext.privileged"=true OR "requestObject.spec.volumes{}.hostPath.path"="/var/run/docker.sock") | table _time user.username verb objectRef.namespace objectRef.name objectRef.resource
ClusterRoleBinding granting elevated rights to Argo CD service account AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-compromise privilege escalation where a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding is created referencing an Argo CD service account and grants cluster-admin or wildcard verbs, consolidating the 'full cluster takeover' the article warns about. Targets the Kubernetes RBAC audit trail. Rationale: The article's stated impact is 'full cluster takeover', which requires elevated RBAC; a new binding tying the argocd SA to cluster-admin is the highest-fidelity signal of that escalation and rarely happens outside of initial install. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9766-5277-j5hr
ATT&CKT1098 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial Argo CD install/upgrade via Helm that legitimately binds the argocd application-controller to broad roles
  • GitOps-managed RBAC where the argocd SA role is declared in Git and reconciled
  • Platform team intentionally granting Argo CD cluster-admin for multi-cluster management
  • Disaster-recovery re-provisioning of the Argo CD namespace
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "helm" and Requestor !has "system:serviceaccount:kube-system"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who (user.username / UserAgent) created the binding — an install via 'helm'/'argocd' user agent during a maintenance window is likely benign; an ad-hoc kubectl or the argocd SA itself creating its own escalation is not. 2) Contain: delete the offending ClusterRoleBinding, revoke/rotate the argocd SA token, and enable network policies. 3) Hunt: review all actions taken by the argocd SA after the binding, enumerate new workloads and secrets accessed, and check Redis cache integrity.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("argocd","argo-cd")
| where ReqStr has_any ("cluster-admin","\"verbs\":[\"*\"]","\"*\"")
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor=tostring(Username), Verb, Res, Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestObject

index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings") | spath | search ("requestObject.subjects{}.name"="*argocd*" OR "requestObject.subjects{}.name"="*argo-cd*") AND ("requestObject.roleRef.name"="cluster-admin" OR "requestObject.roleRef.name"="*admin*") | table _time user.username verb objectRef.name requestObject.roleRef.name requestObject.subjects{}.name
New Argo CD Application/ApplicationSet pointing to external Git repo AIInstallation Medium
Hunts persistence via a backdoored Argo CD Application: creation or mutation of an applications.argoproj.io / applicationsets.argoproj.io resource whose source repoURL points at an external or untrusted Git host, which would let an attacker continuously reconcile malicious manifests into the cluster. Surfaces the repoURL for analyst triage against the org allowlist. Rationale: The attack reconciles workloads from an attacker-controlled Git repo; monitoring Application/ApplicationSet CRD writes and surfacing repoURL lets analysts spot a source pointed at an untrusted host. Left as hunting because the trusted-repo allowlist is org-specific and cannot be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/security/
ATT&CKT1525 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine GitOps onboarding of a new legitimate Application by the platform team
  • App-of-apps pattern generating many child Applications from a template
  • Developers self-servicing new Applications pointed at approved internal GitLab/GitHub Enterprise
  • Migration of Applications between repos during a repo consolidation
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare RepoURL against the approved Git host allowlist; a public/raw-IP or newly registered domain source is suspicious. Confirm who created it (Requestor/UserAgent). 2) Contain: pause auto-sync and delete the Application if the repo is untrusted; enable network policies. 3) Hunt: inspect the manifests that repo would render (privileged specs, external images), correlate with UC3/UC4, and rotate Argo CD repo credentials given CVE-2025-55190/CVE-2026-42880 secret-exposure history.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend Res = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Res in ("applications","applicationsets")
| extend RepoURL = tostring(RequestObject.spec.source.repoURL)
| extend RepoSources = tostring(RequestObject.spec.sources)
| extend RepoTemplate = tostring(RequestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL)
| where isnotempty(RepoURL) or isnotempty(RepoSources) or isnotempty(RepoTemplate)
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor=tostring(Username), Verb, Res, AppName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), RepoURL, RepoTemplate, RepoSources, UserAgent
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(applications OR applicationsets) (@requestObject.spec.source.repoURL:* OR @requestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL:*)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("applications","applicationsets") | spath | eval repoURL=coalesce('requestObject.spec.source.repoURL','requestObject.spec.template.spec.source.repoURL') | where isnotnull(repoURL) | table _time user.username verb objectRef.namespace objectRef.name repoURL

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Suspicious MFA Bypass or MFA Reset Activity · [LLM] Credential Stuffing and Brute Force Against Enterprise Accounts · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Lateral Movement via Valid Compromised Credentials · [LLM] Reconnaissance and Information Gathering Pre-Exploitation · [LLM] Bulk data staging and exfiltration via MEGA / rclone · [LLM] Adversary lurking in incident-response chat tools and calls · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious MFA Bypass or MFA Reset Activity AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Scattered Spider's signature MFA-fatigue / push-bombing pattern: a burst of rejected MFA challenges for a single user followed shortly by a successful sign-in, indicating the user (or a help-desk-reset factor) eventually approved an attacker-driven prompt. Article-specific because the crew's core play is talking help desks into resetting/approving logins rather than breaking software. Rationale: Uses the exact Entra/Azure AD MFA-denied result code 500121 followed by a success inside the same fatigue window — the documented Scattered Spider push-bombing + help-desk-reset signature (CISA AA23-320A). Threshold of 5 rejects/hr is above legitimate user behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1621 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely mis-taps 'Deny' several times on a real prompt before approving
  • Authenticator app time-drift causing repeated failed OTP entries then a correct one
  • Shared/service account where multiple humans trigger prompts for the same identity
  • Poor cellular connectivity dropping push notifications until a retry succeeds
  • Newly enrolled device where the user fumbles first-time MFA setup
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in (dynamic(["<corp egress IPs are known-good; add tenant CIDRs>"])) | where Country !in ("<home country>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AccountUpn's sign-in log around FirstDenial–SuccessTime; check the success IPAddress/Country vs the user's baseline and whether a help-desk password/MFA reset preceded it in AuditLogs. 2) Contain: if the success came from a new IP/geo or an unrecognised device, revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), require password reset, and re-verify the MFA method the user actually controls. 3) Hunt: search AuditLogs for 'Update user'/'security info registered' on the same account, and pivot to any post-auth Teams/SharePoint access from the suspicious IP.
let denials = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 500121   // MFA denied / not completed = push-bombing
| summarize DenialCount = count(), FirstDenial = min(Timestamp), LastDenial = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DenialCount >= 5;      // 5 rejected pushes/hr = fatigue attempt (P99 legit <=2)
let successes = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country;
denials
| join kind=inner successes on AccountUpn
| where SuccessTime between (FirstDenial .. LastDenial + 30m)
| project AccountUpn, FirstDenial, LastDenial, DenialCount, SuccessTime, IPAddress, Country
| order by LastDenial desc
let denials = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500121"   // MFA denied / not completed
| summarize DenialCount = count(), FirstDenial = min(TimeGenerated), LastDenial = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DenialCount >= 5;
let successes = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, LocationDetails;
denials
| join kind=inner successes on UserPrincipalName
| where SuccessTime between (FirstDenial .. LastDenial + 30m)
| project UserPrincipalName, FirstDenial, LastDenial, DenialCount, SuccessTime, IPAddress, LocationDetails
| order by LastDenial desc
